### Foreign data wrapper

**Aliases:** FDW, `FdwRoutine`, `fdwapi.h`, foreign table, foreign server, `postgres_fdw`. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 12, 14, 17, 18, 19.

A foreign data wrapper (FDW) is a plug-in that lets a foreign table read, and optionally write, data that lives outside the local server. The core server passes every operation on a foreign table to its wrapper ([fdwhandler.sgml#fdwhandler](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/fdwhandler.sgml#L11-L19)). A foreign table is a [relation](#relation) with `relkind` `'f'` that has no local storage ([pg_class.h:171](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/catalog/pg_class.h#L171), [pg_class.h#RELKIND_HAS_STORAGE](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/catalog/pg_class.h#L197-L202)). The wrapper's handler function returns an `FdwRoutine`, a table of callbacks for sizing, [path](#path) generation, planning, scanning, modifying and asynchronous execution. `GetFdwRoutine()` calls the handler and checks the result ([fdwapi.h#FdwRoutine](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/foreign/fdwapi.h#L204-L281), [foreign.c#GetFdwRoutine](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/foreign/foreign.c#L321-L345)). The [contrib](#contrib) module `postgres_fdw` is the wrapper for reaching other PostgreSQL servers ([postgres-fdw.sgml:13-15](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/postgres-fdw.sgml#L13-L15), [postgres_fdw.c:553](../raw/postgres-17/contrib/postgres_fdw/postgres_fdw.c#L553)).

**Version notes:**
- PostgreSQL 12: Holds, except that `FdwRoutine` has no asynchronous-execution callbacks ([fdwapi.h#FdwRoutine](../raw/postgres-12/src/include/foreign/fdwapi.h#L183-L249), [pg_class.h:161](../raw/postgres-12/src/include/catalog/pg_class.h#L161), [pg_class.h#RELKIND_HAS_STORAGE](../raw/postgres-12/src/include/catalog/pg_class.h#L187-L192)).
- PostgreSQL 14: Holds. The asynchronous-execution callbacks, such as `IsForeignPathAsyncCapable`, exist as in 17 ([fdwapi.h#FdwRoutine](../raw/postgres-14/src/include/foreign/fdwapi.h#L204-L281), [fdwapi.h:277](../raw/postgres-14/src/include/foreign/fdwapi.h#L277), [pg_class.h#RELKIND_HAS_STORAGE](../raw/postgres-14/src/include/catalog/pg_class.h#L197-L202)).
- PostgreSQL 18: Holds ([fdwapi.h#FdwRoutine](../raw/postgres-18/src/include/foreign/fdwapi.h#L204-L281), [pg_class.h:174](../raw/postgres-18/src/include/catalog/pg_class.h#L174)).
- PostgreSQL 19: Holds. `FdwRoutine` also carries an optional ANALYZE callback, `ImportForeignStatistics` ([fdwapi.h#FdwRoutine](../raw/postgres-19/src/include/foreign/fdwapi.h#L208-L286), [fdwapi.h:160-162](../raw/postgres-19/src/include/foreign/fdwapi.h#L160-L162), [pg_class.h:178](../raw/postgres-19/src/include/catalog/pg_class.h#L178)).

Related: [Contrib](#contrib), [Extension](#extension), [Path](#path), [pg_class](#pg_class)

### Foreign key trigger

**Aliases:** RI trigger, referential integrity trigger, `ri_triggers.c`, `RI_FKey_check`, `RI_FKey_check_ins`, `RI_FKey_noaction_del`. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 12, 14, 17, 18, 19.

A foreign key trigger is one of the internal triggers through which PostgreSQL enforces a foreign key; there is no special executor code for foreign keys. `ri_triggers.c` holds the trigger functions ([ri_triggers.c:3-6](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/adt/ri_triggers.c#L3-L6)). Creating a foreign key adds "check" triggers on the referencing table for `INSERT` and `UPDATE`, and "action" triggers on the referenced table for `DELETE` and `UPDATE` ([tablecmds.c#CreateFKCheckTrigger](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/commands/tablecmds.c#L12345-L12351), [tablecmds.c#createForeignKeyActionTriggers](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/commands/tablecmds.c#L12407-L12414)). The check trigger calls `RI_FKey_check()`. It runs a saved [SPI](#spi) plan for a query of the form `SELECT 1 FROM <pktable> x WHERE pkatt1 = $1 ... FOR KEY SHARE OF x`, building and saving the plan on first use ([ri_triggers.c#RI_FKey_check](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/adt/ri_triggers.c#L234-L239), [ri_triggers.c:346-394](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/adt/ri_triggers.c#L346-L394)). That query takes a key-share [row lock](#row-lock) on the referenced row. When several transactions hold shared locks on one row at once, the row's lockers are recorded as a [MultiXact](#multixact) ([multixact.c:6-8](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/transam/multixact.c#L6-L8)).

**Version notes:**
- PostgreSQL 12: Holds, with the same SPI lookup and `FOR KEY SHARE` lock ([ri_triggers.c:234](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/utils/adt/ri_triggers.c#L234), [ri_triggers.c:356-357](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/utils/adt/ri_triggers.c#L356-L357)).
- PostgreSQL 14: Holds ([ri_triggers.c:236](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/utils/adt/ri_triggers.c#L236), [ri_triggers.c:358-359](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/utils/adt/ri_triggers.c#L358-L359)).
- PostgreSQL 18: Holds, with the same SPI lookup and `FOR KEY SHARE` lock ([ri_triggers.c:371-372](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/utils/adt/ri_triggers.c#L371-L372)). New in 18: temporal foreign keys that use `PERIOD` ([ri_triggers.c:124](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/utils/adt/ri_triggers.c#L124)).
- PostgreSQL 19: Differs: `RI_FKey_check()` has a fast path that probes the referenced unique index directly and skips SPI ([ri_triggers.c#RI_FKey_check](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/utils/adt/ri_triggers.c#L424-L437)). It applies when the referenced table is not partitioned and the key is not temporal (temporal keys exist as in 18) ([ri_triggers.c#ri_fastpath_is_applicable](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/utils/adt/ri_triggers.c#L2987-L3011)). After locking the referenced table and opening its index, it also requires a B-tree index whose key collations match the referenced columns and whose opfamily still treats the constraint's operator as equality; otherwise the check falls back to SPI ([ri_triggers.c#ri_check_fastpath_index](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/utils/adt/ri_triggers.c#L3013-L3091)). It checks one row per call, takes its snapshot only after that lock, and calls `ri_CheckPermissions()` on the referenced table ([ri_triggers.c#ri_FastPathCheck](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/utils/adt/ri_triggers.c#L2758-L2834)). The fast path still takes a key-share lock on the referenced row ([ri_triggers.c#ri_LockPKTuple](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/utils/adt/ri_triggers.c#L2922-L2936)). Other keys still use the SPI query ([ri_triggers.c:462-463](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/utils/adt/ri_triggers.c#L462-L463)).

Related: [MultiXact](#multixact), [Row lock](#row-lock), [SPI](#spi), [Heavyweight lock](#heavyweight-lock)

### Fork

**Aliases:** relation fork, `ForkNumber`, main fork. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 12, 14, 17, 18, 19.

A fork is one of the separate file sets that make up a single [relation](#relation)'s storage. The main fork holds the data. The [free space map](#free-space-map) and [visibility map](#visibility-map) are secondary forks. Unlogged relations also have an init fork ([glossary.sgml#glossary-fork](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/glossary.sgml#L799-L811)). In source, the `ForkNumber` enum names them `MAIN_FORKNUM`, `FSM_FORKNUM`, `VISIBILITYMAP_FORKNUM` and `INIT_FORKNUM`. Buffer and storage calls such as `ReadBufferExtended()` take one of these values ([relpath.h#ForkNumber](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/common/relpath.h#L47-L62), [bufmgr.c#ReadBufferExtended](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/storage/buffer/bufmgr.c#L799-L800)).

**Version notes:**
- PostgreSQL 12: Holds. The main, FSM, visibility-map and init forks exist with the same `ForkNumber` names, and `ReadBufferExtended()` takes a fork ([relpath.h#ForkNumber](../raw/postgres-12/src/include/common/relpath.h#L40-L53), [bufmgr.c:641](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/storage/buffer/bufmgr.c#L641)). 12 has no `glossary.sgml`; `storage.sgml` describes the forks ([storage.sgml:205-216](../raw/postgres-12/doc/src/sgml/storage.sgml#L205-L216)).
- PostgreSQL 14: Holds. The same four forks exist in `ForkNumber`, and unlogged relations have an init fork ([relpath.h#ForkNumber](../raw/postgres-14/src/include/common/relpath.h#L40-L53), [glossary.sgml#glossary-fork](../raw/postgres-14/doc/src/sgml/glossary.sgml#L635-L648)).
- PostgreSQL 18: Holds ([glossary.sgml#glossary-fork](../raw/postgres-18/doc/src/sgml/glossary.sgml#L824-L836), [relpath.h#ForkNumber](../raw/postgres-18/src/include/common/relpath.h#L56-L71)).
- PostgreSQL 19: Holds. The glossary still lists main, FSM, VM and init forks, and `ForkNumber` has the same four members ([glossary.sgml#glossary-fork](../raw/postgres-19/doc/src/sgml/glossary.sgml#L839-L852), [relpath.h#ForkNumber](../raw/postgres-19/src/include/common/relpath.h#L56-L69), [bufmgr.c:926](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/storage/buffer/bufmgr.c#L926)).

Related: [Free space map](#free-space-map), [Relfilenumber](#relfilenumber), [Visibility map](#visibility-map)

### Free space map

**Aliases:** FSM, `FSM_FORKNUM`. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 12, 14, 17, 18, 19.

The free space map (FSM) records roughly how much free space each page of a [relation](#relation) has, so an insert can find a page with room without scanning the table. It lives in its own [fork](#fork), used by all heaps and by the index access methods that need it ([glossary.sgml#glossary-fsm](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/glossary.sgml#L814-L828), [freespace.c:16-20](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/storage/freespace/freespace.c#L16-L20)). It stores one byte per page, as one of 256 space categories ([freespace.c:36-42](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/storage/freespace/freespace.c#L36-L42)). In code, `GetPageWithFreeSpace()` finds a page with enough room, `RecordPageWithFreeSpace()` updates one page's entry, and `FreeSpaceMapVacuum()` updates the upper levels of the map. Until the upper levels are updated, newly recorded free space may be invisible to searchers ([freespace.c#GetPageWithFreeSpace](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/storage/freespace/freespace.c#L120-L137), [freespace.c#RecordPageWithFreeSpace](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/storage/freespace/freespace.c#L186-L194), [freespace.c#FreeSpaceMapVacuum](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/storage/freespace/freespace.c#L361-L368)). Do not confuse it with the [visibility map](#visibility-map), a different fork that tracks tuple visibility per page ([glossary.sgml#glossary-vm](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/glossary.sgml#L2093-L2105)).

**Version notes:**
- PostgreSQL 12: Holds. The FSM lives in its own fork and stores one byte per page as one of 256 categories ([freespace.c:16-20](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/storage/freespace/freespace.c#L16-L20), [freespace.c:35-41](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/storage/freespace/freespace.c#L35-L41)). `GetPageWithFreeSpace()`, `RecordPageWithFreeSpace()` and `FreeSpaceMapVacuum()` are the entry points ([freespace.c#GetPageWithFreeSpace](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/storage/freespace/freespace.c#L118-L132), [freespace.c#RecordPageWithFreeSpace](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/storage/freespace/freespace.c#L173-L181), [freespace.c#FreeSpaceMapVacuum](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/storage/freespace/freespace.c#L342-L349)). 12 has no `glossary.sgml`; `storage.sgml` describes the FSM and VM forks ([storage.sgml:205-213](../raw/postgres-12/doc/src/sgml/storage.sgml#L205-L213)).
- PostgreSQL 14: Holds. The FSM uses one byte per page in 256 categories, with the same three entry points ([glossary.sgml#glossary-fsm](../raw/postgres-14/doc/src/sgml/glossary.sgml#L650-L665), [freespace.c:35-41](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/storage/freespace/freespace.c#L35-L41), [freespace.c#GetPageWithFreeSpace](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/storage/freespace/freespace.c#L119-L136), [freespace.c#RecordPageWithFreeSpace](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/storage/freespace/freespace.c#L185-L193), [freespace.c#FreeSpaceMapVacuum](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/storage/freespace/freespace.c#L359-L366)).
- PostgreSQL 18: Holds ([glossary.sgml#glossary-fsm](../raw/postgres-18/doc/src/sgml/glossary.sgml#L839-L853), [freespace.c:36-42](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/storage/freespace/freespace.c#L36-L42), [freespace.c#GetPageWithFreeSpace](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/storage/freespace/freespace.c#L120-L137), [freespace.c#RecordPageWithFreeSpace](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/storage/freespace/freespace.c#L186-L194), [freespace.c#FreeSpaceMapVacuum](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/storage/freespace/freespace.c#L361-L368)).
- PostgreSQL 19: Holds. The FSM still stores one byte per page in 256 categories, and `GetPageWithFreeSpace()`, `RecordPageWithFreeSpace()` and `FreeSpaceMapVacuum()` are unchanged ([glossary.sgml#glossary-fsm](../raw/postgres-19/doc/src/sgml/glossary.sgml#L854-L869), [freespace.c:36-42](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/storage/freespace/freespace.c#L36-L42), [freespace.c#GetPageWithFreeSpace](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/storage/freespace/freespace.c#L120-L137), [freespace.c#RecordPageWithFreeSpace](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/storage/freespace/freespace.c#L186-L194), [freespace.c#FreeSpaceMapVacuum](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/storage/freespace/freespace.c#L351-L358), [glossary.sgml#glossary-vm](../raw/postgres-19/doc/src/sgml/glossary.sgml#L2209-L2222)).

Related: [Fork](#fork), [pg_freespacemap](#pg_freespacemap), [Visibility map](#visibility-map)

### Freezing

**Checked on:** PostgreSQL 12, 14, 17, 18, 19.

Freezing marks an old row version as frozen, which means its inserting transaction is certain to be visible to all current and future transactions. A frozen row version counts as older than every normal [transaction ID](#transaction-id) (xid), so it stays "in the past" after the xid counter [wraps around](#wraparound) ([maintenance.sgml#vacuum-for-wraparound](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/maintenance.sgml#L434-L456)). VACUUM freezes rows, and table rewrites such as [VACUUM FULL](#vacuum-full) and [CLUSTER](#cluster) freeze eligible rows as they copy them ([rewriteheap.c#rewrite_heap_tuple](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/heap/rewriteheap.c#L367-L375)). The reserved `FrozenTransactionId` (2) marks very old tuples ([transam.h#FrozenTransactionId](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/access/transam.h#L20-L35)). Since PostgreSQL 9.4, freezing sets the `HEAP_XMIN_FROZEN` infomask bits and keeps the original `t_xmin` for forensic use, instead of overwriting it with `FrozenTransactionId`. Rows frozen the old way can still appear in clusters upgraded with [pg_upgrade](#pg_upgrade) from before 9.4 ([maintenance.sgml:462-469](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/maintenance.sgml#L462-L469), [heapam.c:7612-7616](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/heap/heapam.c#L7612-L7616), [htup_details.h:206](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/access/htup_details.h#L206)). `heap_prepare_freeze_tuple()` checks a tuple's xmin, xmax and xvac against the freeze cutoffs and prepares a per-tuple freeze plan ([heapam.c#heap_prepare_freeze_tuple](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/heap/heapam.c#L7371-L7415)). Its caller then decides whether to freeze the whole page. It must freeze when an xid or [MultiXact](#multixact) ID older than the cutoffs is present. Otherwise it freezes only when that makes the page all-frozen and a [full-page image](#full-page-image) of the page has been, or will be, written anyway ([pruneheap.c#heap_page_prune_and_freeze](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/heap/pruneheap.c#L669-L722)). `vacuum_freeze_min_age`, the minimum xid age before VACUUM freezes a row version, has context `user`, so it can be set per session or transaction ([guc_tables.c#vacuum_freeze_min_age](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L2666-L2672)).

**Version notes:**
- PostgreSQL 12: Differs: 12 has no page-level freeze decision. `heap_prepare_freeze_tuple()` fills a per-tuple `*frz` entry for each tuple whose xids cross the cutoffs, and VACUUM applies and WAL-logs every such entry on the page ([heapam.c#heap_prepare_freeze_tuple](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/heap/heapam.c#L6085-L6118), [vacuumlazy.c#lazy_scan_heap](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c#L1186-L1195), [vacuumlazy.c#lazy_scan_heap](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c#L1207-L1231)). The rest holds: rewrites freeze rows, frozen rows count as older than every normal xid, and freezing sets `HEAP_XMIN_FROZEN` and keeps `t_xmin` ([rewriteheap.c#rewrite_heap_tuple](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/heap/rewriteheap.c#L405-L413), [maintenance.sgml#vacuum-for-wraparound](../raw/postgres-12/doc/src/sgml/maintenance.sgml#L400-L413), [maintenance.sgml:437-444](../raw/postgres-12/doc/src/sgml/maintenance.sgml#L437-L444), [heapam.c:6162](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/heap/heapam.c#L6162), [transam.h#FrozenTransactionId](../raw/postgres-12/src/include/access/transam.h#L20-L34)). `vacuum_freeze_min_age` is `PGC_USERSET` (session scope) ([guc.c#vacuum_freeze_min_age](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L2411-L2413)).
- PostgreSQL 14: Differs: 14 has no page-level freeze decision. `lazy_scan_prune()` asks `heap_prepare_freeze_tuple()` for a per-tuple `xl_heap_freeze_tuple` entry, then applies every entry on the page with `heap_execute_freeze_tuple()` and WAL-logs them with `log_heap_freeze()` ([heapam.c#heap_prepare_freeze_tuple](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/heap/heapam.c#L7009-L7012), [vacuumlazy.c#lazy_scan_prune](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c#L1929-L1935), [vacuumlazy.c#lazy_scan_prune](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c#L1961-L1995)). The rest holds: rewrites freeze rows, frozen rows count as older than every normal xid, and freezing sets `HEAP_XMIN_FROZEN` and keeps `t_xmin` ([rewriteheap.c#rewrite_heap_tuple](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/heap/rewriteheap.c#L387-L395), [maintenance.sgml#vacuum-for-wraparound](../raw/postgres-14/doc/src/sgml/maintenance.sgml#L435-L456), [maintenance.sgml:462-469](../raw/postgres-14/doc/src/sgml/maintenance.sgml#L462-L469), [heapam.c:7053](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/heap/heapam.c#L7053), [transam.h#FrozenTransactionId](../raw/postgres-14/src/include/access/transam.h#L24-L33)). `vacuum_freeze_min_age` is `PGC_USERSET` (session scope) ([guc.c:2618](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L2618)).
- PostgreSQL 18: Holds ([transam.h#FrozenTransactionId](../raw/postgres-18/src/include/access/transam.h#L20-L35), [heapam.c:7517](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/access/heap/heapam.c#L7517), [htup_details.h:206](../raw/postgres-18/src/include/access/htup_details.h#L206), [heapam.c#heap_prepare_freeze_tuple](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/access/heap/heapam.c#L7272-L7316), [pruneheap.c#heap_page_prune_and_freeze](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/access/heap/pruneheap.c#L669-L722), [rewriteheap.c#rewrite_heap_tuple](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/access/heap/rewriteheap.c#L367-L375)). `vacuum_freeze_min_age` is still `user` context (session scope) ([guc_tables.c#vacuum_freeze_min_age](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L2794-L2801)). New in 18: a normal (non-aggressive) vacuum may also scan some all-visible pages eagerly, to freeze them ahead of the next aggressive vacuum ([vacuumlazy.c:54-58](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c#L54-L58)). `vacuum_max_eager_freeze_failure_rate` (default 0.03; 0 disables eager scanning) bounds this. Its context is `user` (session scope) ([guc_tables.c#vacuum_max_eager_freeze_failure_rate](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L4155-L4162)).
- PostgreSQL 19: Holds. The page-level freeze decision moved into `heap_page_will_freeze()`, with the same rules ([pruneheap.c#heap_page_will_freeze](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/access/heap/pruneheap.c#L751-L829)). As in 18, a normal vacuum may eagerly scan some all-visible pages to freeze them, bounded by `vacuum_max_eager_freeze_failure_rate` (context `user`, session scope) ([vacuumlazy.c:54-58](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c#L54-L58), [guc_parameters.dat#vacuum_max_eager_freeze_failure_rate](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_parameters.dat#L3396-L3403)). `FrozenTransactionId` is still 2, frozen tuples still use the `HEAP_XMIN_FROZEN` bits, rewrites still freeze rows, and `vacuum_freeze_min_age` is still `PGC_USERSET` (session scope) ([maintenance.sgml:471-478](../raw/postgres-19/doc/src/sgml/maintenance.sgml#L471-L478), [transam.h#FrozenTransactionId](../raw/postgres-19/src/include/access/transam.h#L23-L33), [heapam.c:7480](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/access/heap/heapam.c#L7480), [heapam.c#heap_prepare_freeze_tuple](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/access/heap/heapam.c#L7223-L7276), [rewriteheap.c#rewrite_heap_tuple](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/access/heap/rewriteheap.c#L368-L376), [guc_parameters.dat#vacuum_freeze_min_age](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_parameters.dat#L3380-L3386)).

Related: [Transaction ID](#transaction-id), [Wraparound](#wraparound), [xmin and xmax](#xmin-and-xmax), [VACUUM](#vacuum), [MultiXact](#multixact)

### fsync

**Aliases:** `fsync()`, `pg_fsync`, durable flush, `fsync` setting, `data_sync_retry`. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 12, 14, 17, 18, 19.

`fsync` is the system call PostgreSQL issues to make data it has already written to a file durable on disk. The same name is used for the setting that enables those calls ([config.sgml#guc-fsync](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/config.sgml#L3022-L3035)). Wrappers in `fd.c` make the calls: `pg_fsync()` flushes a file, and `pg_flush_data()` only advises the OS to start writing dirty data early, so that a later `fsync` costs less ([fd.c#pg_fsync](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/storage/file/fd.c#L385-L389), [fd.c#pg_flush_data](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/storage/file/fd.c#L518-L530)). A backend that writes a data file segment usually does not flush it. `register_dirty_segment()` hands the fsync request to the [checkpointer](#checkpointer), and does the fsync itself only if that fails ([md.c#register_dirty_segment](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/storage/smgr/md.c#L1359-L1369)). At a [checkpoint](#checkpoint), `CheckPointGuts()` writes out dirty buffers and then calls `ProcessSyncRequests()` to flush every queued file ([xlog.c#CheckPointGuts](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/transam/xlog.c#L7530-L7535)). A failed data-file fsync makes the server `PANIC` unless `data_sync_retry` is on, because the OS may already have dropped the dirty data ([fd.c#data_sync_elevel](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/storage/file/fd.c#L3918-L3936)). The `fsync` setting has context `sighup`, so changing it needs a reload. Turning it off risks unrecoverable corruption after a crash ([guc_tables.c:1096-1107](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L1096-L1107), [config.sgml#guc-fsync](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/config.sgml#L3037-L3044)). `data_sync_retry` has context `postmaster` and needs a restart ([guc_tables.c:2003](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L2003)).

**Version notes:**
- PostgreSQL 12: Holds, except that `CheckPointBuffers()`, not `CheckPointGuts()`, calls `ProcessSyncRequests()` after `BufferSync()` ([bufmgr.c#CheckPointBuffers](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/storage/buffer/bufmgr.c#L2572-L2591), [xlog.c#CheckPointGuts](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/transam/xlog.c#L8995-L9010)). `fsync` (context `sighup`) and `data_sync_retry` (context `postmaster`) are defined in `guc.c` ([guc.c:1123](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L1123), [guc.c:1947](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L1947)), and the `fd.c` wrappers and the sync request queue exist ([fd.c:333](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/storage/file/fd.c#L333), [fd.c:405](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/storage/file/fd.c#L405), [sync.c:236](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/storage/sync/sync.c#L236)).
- PostgreSQL 14: Holds ([guc.c:1228](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L1228), [fd.c:352](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/storage/file/fd.c#L352), [sync.c:294](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/storage/sync/sync.c#L294)).
- PostgreSQL 18: Holds ([guc_tables.c:1136](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L1136), [fd.c:389](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/storage/file/fd.c#L389), [sync.c:286](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/storage/sync/sync.c#L286)).
- PostgreSQL 19: Holds; `fsync` is declared in `guc_parameters.dat`, context `sighup` ([guc_parameters.dat:1109](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_parameters.dat#L1109), [fd.c:390](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/storage/file/fd.c#L390), [sync.c:287](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/storage/sync/sync.c#L287)).

### Full-page image

**Aliases:** FPI, full-page write, backup block. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 12, 14, 17, 18, 19.

A full-page image (FPI) is a copy of a whole data page stored inside a [WAL](#wal) record. Replay restores the copy instead of redoing a small change, which guards against pages left half-written by a crash ([transam/README:424-435](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/transam/README#L424-L435)). By default, the first change to a page after a [checkpoint](#checkpoint) carries one. `XLogRecordAssemble()` adds an image when the block is registered with `REGBUF_FORCE_IMAGE`, or when the page [LSN](#lsn) is at or before `RedoRecPtr`, unless `REGBUF_NO_IMAGE` is set or page writes are off ([xloginsert.c#XLogRecordAssemble](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/transam/xloginsert.c#L604-L620)). Page writes stay on while a base backup runs, even when `full_page_writes` is off ([xlog.c:847](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/transam/xlog.c#L847), [xlog.c:8896](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/transam/xlog.c#L8896)). `log_newpage()` uses `REGBUF_FORCE_IMAGE` to log a whole page as its own record, outside the first-change rule ([xloginsert.c#log_newpage](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/transam/xloginsert.c#L1143-L1155)). `full_page_writes` has context `sighup`, so changing it needs a reload ([guc_tables.c#full_page_writes](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L1157-L1167)).

**Version notes:**
- PostgreSQL 12: Holds. The first change to a page after a checkpoint carries a full-page copy, and `XLogRecordAssemble()` makes the same `REGBUF_FORCE_IMAGE`, `REGBUF_NO_IMAGE` and LSN tests ([transam/README:418-426](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/transam/README#L418-L426), [xloginsert.c#XLogRecordAssemble](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/transam/xloginsert.c#L539-L555)). A base backup keeps page writes on by setting `forcePageWrites`, and `log_newpage()` forces an image ([xlog.c:1053](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/transam/xlog.c#L1053), [xlog.c:10278](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/transam/xlog.c#L10278), [xloginsert.c:978](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/transam/xloginsert.c#L978)). `full_page_writes` is `PGC_SIGHUP` (reload) ([guc.c#full_page_writes](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L1164-L1166)).
- PostgreSQL 14: Holds. The first change to a page after a checkpoint carries a page copy, and `XLogRecordAssemble()` makes the same `REGBUF_FORCE_IMAGE`, `REGBUF_NO_IMAGE` and LSN tests ([transam/README:424-435](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/transam/README#L424-L435), [xloginsert.c#XLogRecordAssemble](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/transam/xloginsert.c#L547-L563)). A base backup keeps page writes on by setting `forcePageWrites`, and `log_newpage()` forces an image ([xlog.c:1117](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/transam/xlog.c#L1117), [xlog.c:11233](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/transam/xlog.c#L11233), [xloginsert.c:1002](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/transam/xloginsert.c#L1002)). `full_page_writes` is `PGC_SIGHUP`, so a change needs a reload ([guc.c:1288](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L1288)).
- PostgreSQL 18: Holds ([transam/README:424-435](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/access/transam/README#L424-L435), [xloginsert.c#XLogRecordAssemble](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/access/transam/xloginsert.c#L604-L620), [xlog.c:846](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/access/transam/xlog.c#L846), [xlog.c:8892](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/access/transam/xlog.c#L8892), [xloginsert.c#log_newpage](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/access/transam/xloginsert.c#L1143-L1155)). `full_page_writes` is still `sighup` (reload) ([guc_tables.c#full_page_writes](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L1196-L1206)).
- PostgreSQL 19: Holds. The first-change rule, the `REGBUF_FORCE_IMAGE`, `REGBUF_NO_IMAGE` and LSN tests, the base-backup override and `log_newpage()` are unchanged ([transam/README:424-435](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/access/transam/README#L424-L435), [xloginsert.c#XLogRecordAssemble](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/access/transam/xloginsert.c#L678-L694), [xlog.c:883](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/access/transam/xlog.c#L883), [xlog.c:9060](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/access/transam/xlog.c#L9060), [xloginsert.c#log_newpage](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/access/transam/xloginsert.c#L1191-L1203)). `full_page_writes` is still `PGC_SIGHUP` (reload) ([guc_parameters.dat#full_page_writes](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_parameters.dat#L1116-L1121)).

### Function volatility

**Aliases:** volatility category, `IMMUTABLE`, `STABLE`, `VOLATILE`, `provolatile`, `PROVOLATILE_IMMUTABLE`. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 12, 14, 17, 18, 19.

Function volatility is the promise a function makes to the planner about how its result can change. `VOLATILE`, the default, promises nothing and is re-evaluated for every row. `STABLE` promises the same result for the same arguments within one statement. `IMMUTABLE` promises the same result forever ([xfunc.sgml#xfunc-volatility](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/xfunc.sgml#L1610-L1667)). The catalog stores it in `pg_proc.provolatile` as `'i'`, `'s'` or `'v'` ([pg_proc.h#PROVOLATILE_IMMUTABLE](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/catalog/pg_proc.h#L158-L166)). The [planner](#planner) acts on it. `evaluate_function()` folds an immutable call with constant arguments to a constant, and it folds a stable call only when it is estimating ([clauses.c#evaluate_function](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/clauses.c#L4495-L4507)). `contain_volatile_functions()` blocks optimizations such as inlining a [common table expression](#common-table-expression) (CTE) ([clauses.c:535](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/clauses.c#L535), [subselect.c#SS_process_ctes](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/plan/subselect.c#L941-L949)). `CREATE INDEX` rejects an [index expression](#expression-index) that calls any function that is not immutable ([indexcmds.c:1960-1966](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/commands/indexcmds.c#L1960-L1966)).

**Version notes:**
- PostgreSQL 12: Holds ([pg_proc.h#PROVOLATILE_IMMUTABLE](../raw/postgres-12/src/include/catalog/pg_proc.h#L154-L156), [xfunc.sgml#xfunc-volatility](../raw/postgres-12/doc/src/sgml/xfunc.sgml#L1499-L1537), [clauses.c:4348](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/optimizer/util/clauses.c#L4348), [subselect.c:897](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/optimizer/plan/subselect.c#L897), [indexcmds.c:1660](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/commands/indexcmds.c#L1660)).
- PostgreSQL 14: Holds ([pg_proc.h#PROVOLATILE_IMMUTABLE](../raw/postgres-14/src/include/catalog/pg_proc.h#L163-L165), [xfunc.sgml#xfunc-volatility](../raw/postgres-14/doc/src/sgml/xfunc.sgml#L1625-L1663), [clauses.c:4335](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/optimizer/util/clauses.c#L4335), [subselect.c:962](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/optimizer/plan/subselect.c#L962), [indexcmds.c:1918](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/commands/indexcmds.c#L1918)).

### GEQO

**Aliases:** genetic query optimizer, genetic query optimization, `geqo`, `geqo_threshold`, `geqo()`. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 17, 18, 19.

GEQO (the genetic query optimizer) is the [planner](#planner)'s fallback join search for queries that join many relations. The exhaustive join search takes too long there, so GEQO treats join order like a traveling-salesman problem. It encodes each candidate join order as a string of relation numbers and evolves a pool of such orders instead of trying them all ([geqo.sgml#geqo-pg-intro](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/geqo.sgml#L109-L125), [geqo_main.c#geqo](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/geqo/geqo_main.c#L66-L72)). `make_rel_from_joinlist()` calls `geqo()` instead of `standard_join_search()` when no `join_search_hook` is set, `geqo` is on and the number of `FROM` items reaches `geqo_threshold` ([allpaths.c:3374](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/allpaths.c#L3374)). `geqo` defaults to on and `geqo_threshold` to 12; both are `PGC_USERSET`, so they apply at session or transaction scope ([guc_tables.c:1011-1018](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L1011-L1018), [guc_tables.c:2107-2113](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L2107-L2113), [config.sgml#guc-geqo-threshold](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/config.sgml#L6158-L6172)). `geqo_eval()` scores a join order by the total cost of the cheapest path it builds, or `DBL_MAX` when no valid plan exists, and the pool keeps that score as each chromosome's `Cost` worth ([geqo_eval.c#geqo_eval](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/geqo/geqo_eval.c#L56-L57), [geqo_eval.c:115-118](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/geqo/geqo_eval.c#L115-L118), [geqo_gene.h:35](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/optimizer/geqo_gene.h#L35)).

**Version notes:**
- PostgreSQL 18: Holds. The call site, the two GUCs and their defaults are unchanged, and `geqo_eval()` still scores a join order by total cost alone, even though 18 paths also count `disabled_nodes` ([allpaths.c:3424-3425](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/optimizer/path/allpaths.c#L3424-L3425), [guc_tables.c:1050](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L1050), [guc_tables.c:2224](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L2224), [geqo_eval.c:115-118](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/optimizer/geqo/geqo_eval.c#L115-L118), [geqo_gene.h:35](../raw/postgres-18/src/include/optimizer/geqo_gene.h#L35)).
- PostgreSQL 19: Differs in the score. A join order's fitness is now a `Fitness` pair of `disabled_nodes` and `cost`, and `fitness_compare()` prefers fewer disabled nodes before lower cost, the way `add_path()` ranks paths ([pathnode.c#add_path](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/optimizer/util/pathnode.c#L395-L405)); an invalid order gets `INT_MAX` disabled nodes and `DBL_MAX` cost ([geqo_gene.h#Fitness](../raw/postgres-19/src/include/optimizer/geqo_gene.h#L38-L70), [geqo_eval.c:108-121](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/optimizer/geqo/geqo_eval.c#L108-L121), [geqo_pool.c:148](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/optimizer/geqo/geqo_pool.c#L148)). So a join order whose cheapest plan uses a disabled path type, for example a sequential scan under `enable_seqscan = off`, now loses to any order whose plan avoids one. The call site and both GUCs are unchanged; they are defined in `guc_parameters.dat` ([allpaths.c:3905-3906](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/optimizer/path/allpaths.c#L3905-L3906), [guc_parameters.dat#geqo](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_parameters.dat#L1123-L1129), [guc_parameters.dat#geqo_threshold](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_parameters.dat#L1178-L1185)).

Related: [Planner](#planner), [Path](#path), [pgs_mask](#pgs_mask), [GUC context](#guc-context)

### GIN

**Aliases:** Generalized Inverted Index. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 12, 14, 17, 18, 19.

GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) is an inverted index. It maps each key found inside a value, such as an array element or a text-search lexeme, to the list of rows that contain it ([gin/README:8-26](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/gin/README#L8-L26)). A GIN index has a [metapage](#metapage) and a B-tree of key entries. A key's row list is stored either inline as a [posting list](#posting-list) or as a separate [posting tree](#posting-tree). If `fastupdate` is on, the index can also have [pending-list](#pending-list) pages ([gin/README:95-105](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/gin/README#L95-L105)). GIN sets `amgettuple` and `amcanreturn` to NULL, so it supports neither plain [index scans](#index-scan) nor [index-only scans](#index-only-scan); it returns matches only through `amgetbitmap`, for [bitmap scans](#bitmap-scan) ([ginutil.c:70-80](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/gin/ginutil.c#L70-L80)).

**Version notes:**
- PostgreSQL 12: Holds. GIN has a metapage, a B-tree of keys, posting trees, and fast-update pending pages, and it leaves `amgettuple` and `amcanreturn` NULL ([gin/README:8-12](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/gin/README#L8-L12), [gin/README:95-105](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/gin/README#L95-L105), [ginutil.c:63-71](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/gin/ginutil.c#L63-L71)).
- PostgreSQL 14: Holds. The README describes the same inverted index, with a metapage, a B-tree of key entries, posting lists or posting trees, and pending-list pages under fast update; `amgettuple` and `amcanreturn` are NULL ([gin/README:8-26](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/gin/README#L8-L26), [gin/README:95-105](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/gin/README#L95-L105), [ginutil.c:68-77](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/gin/ginutil.c#L68-L77)).
- PostgreSQL 18: Holds. GIN still sets `amcanreturn` and `amgettuple` to NULL ([gin/README:8-26](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/access/gin/README#L8-L26), [ginutil.c:74-84](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/access/gin/ginutil.c#L74-L84)). New in 18: `ginhandler()` sets `amcanbuildparallel`, so GIN indexes can be built in parallel ([ginutil.c:60](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/access/gin/ginutil.c#L60), [gininsert.c#GinBuildShared](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/access/gin/gininsert.c#L49-L96)).
- PostgreSQL 19: Holds. GIN is still an inverted index of keys to posting lists or posting trees, with a metapage and optional pending-list pages, and it still sets `amgettuple` and `amcanreturn` to NULL ([gin/README:8-26](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/access/gin/README#L8-L26), [gin/README:95-105](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/access/gin/README#L95-L105), [ginutil.c:75](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/access/gin/ginutil.c#L75), [ginutil.c:85](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/access/gin/ginutil.c#L85)). As in 18, `ginhandler()` sets `amcanbuildparallel`, so GIN indexes can be built in parallel ([ginutil.c:61](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/access/gin/ginutil.c#L61)).

Related: [Posting list](#posting-list), [Posting tree](#posting-tree), [Pending list](#pending-list), [Bitmap scan](#bitmap-scan), [Access method](#access-method)

### GiST

**Aliases:** Generalized Search Tree. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 12, 14, 17, 18, 19.

GiST (Generalized Search Tree) is a balanced tree framework for building custom index types, such as R-trees for geometric data ([gist.sgml#gist-intro](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/gist.sgml#L11-L25), [gist/README:1-25](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/gist/README#L1-L25)). The GiST core handles concurrency, WAL logging and tree search. The [operator class](#operator-class) supplies the data type's semantics through support methods such as `consistent`, `union`, `penalty` and `picksplit` ([gist.sgml#gist-extensibility](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/gist.sgml#L224-L232), [gist.sgml#gist-extensibility](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/gist.sgml#L268-L274)). In PostgreSQL 17, `gisthandler()` marks GiST as supporting ordered nearest-neighbor searches and multicolumn keys, but not unique indexes ([gist.c#gisthandler](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/gist/gist.c#L59-L70)). GiST keeps its root at block 0, and a root split replaces that page's contents in place ([gist_private.h:262](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/access/gist_private.h#L262), [gist/README:177-180](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/gist/README#L177-L180)).

**Version notes:**
- PostgreSQL 12: Holds. `gisthandler()` sets `amcanorderbyop` and `amcanmulticol` true and `amcanunique` false, the operator class supplies the semantics, block 0 is the root, and a root split rewrites it in place ([gist.c#gisthandler](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/gist/gist.c#L59-L69), [gist.sgml#gist-intro](../raw/postgres-12/doc/src/sgml/gist.sgml#L11-L25), [gist.sgml#gist-extensibility](../raw/postgres-12/doc/src/sgml/gist.sgml#L226-L234), [gist_private.h:263](../raw/postgres-12/src/include/access/gist_private.h#L263), [gist/README:175-178](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/gist/README#L175-L178)).
- PostgreSQL 14: Holds. `gisthandler()` sets ordered nearest-neighbour search and multicolumn support but not uniqueness, block 0 is the root, and a root split rewrites it in place ([gist.sgml#gist-intro](../raw/postgres-14/doc/src/sgml/gist.sgml#L11-L25), [gist.c#gisthandler](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/gist/gist.c#L67-L70), [gist_private.h:262](../raw/postgres-14/src/include/access/gist_private.h#L262), [gist/README:176-179](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/gist/README#L176-L179)).
- PostgreSQL 18: Holds. `gisthandler()` still sets ordered nearest-neighbor search and multicolumn support, but not uniqueness, and block 0 is still the root ([gist.c#gisthandler](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/access/gist/gist.c#L59-L73), [gist_private.h:262](../raw/postgres-18/src/include/access/gist_private.h#L262), [gist/README:177-180](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/access/gist/README#L177-L180)).
- PostgreSQL 19: Holds. `gisthandler()` still marks ordered nearest-neighbor search and multicolumn support but no uniqueness, and block 0 is still the root ([gist.sgml#gist-intro](../raw/postgres-19/doc/src/sgml/gist.sgml#L11-L25), [gist/README:1-25](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/access/gist/README#L1-L25), [gist.c#gisthandler](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/access/gist/gist.c#L59-L73), [gist_private.h:262](../raw/postgres-19/src/include/access/gist_private.h#L262), [gist/README:184-187](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/access/gist/README#L184-L187)).
