### GiST build method

**Aliases:** sorted build, buffering build, `buffering` storage parameter, `GIST_SORTSUPPORT_PROC`, `GistBuildMode`. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 12, 14, 17, 18, 19.

A [GiST](#gist) index can be built in two ways. A sorted build sorts all tuples and packs leaf pages bottom-up, as a B-tree build does. An insert build adds tuples one at a time and may switch to a buffering algorithm that queues tuples at inner levels to cut I/O ([gistbuild.c:6-22](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/gist/gistbuild.c#L6-L22)). `gistbuild()` uses the sorted method only when every key column's [operator class](#operator-class) supplies a `sortsupport` function (`GIST_SORTSUPPORT_PROC`) and the `buffering` [storage parameter](#storage-parameter) is not `on` ([gistbuild.c#gistbuild](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/gist/gistbuild.c#L209-L247), [gist.h:40](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/access/gist.h#L40)). `buffering` accepts `on`, `off` and `auto`, and `auto` is the default ([reloptions.c:521-531](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/common/reloptions.c#L521-L531)). `gistbuild()` turns [fillfactor](#fillfactor) into a free-space target ([gistbuild.c:253-254](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/gist/gistbuild.c#L253-L254)). Only the insert path, buffered or not, leaves that space free on each page ([gistbuild.c:863-864](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/gist/gistbuild.c#L863-L864), [gistbuild.c:1063-1064](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/gist/gistbuild.c#L1063-L1064)). The sorted build ignores fillfactor: it fills pages completely, and when it has filled several it redistributes their tuples with the operator class's picksplit method ([gistbuild.c#gist_indexsortbuild_levelstate_add](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/gist/gistbuild.c#L466-L468), [gistbuild.c#gist_indexsortbuild_levelstate_flush](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/gist/gistbuild.c#L509-L524)).

**Version notes:**
- PostgreSQL 12: Differs: only the insert build exists, with optional buffering; `GistBufferingMode` has no sorted mode ([gistbuild.c#GistBufferingMode](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/gist/gistbuild.c#L43-L54)). The v12 support-function numbers in `gist.h` stop at `GIST_FETCH_PROC` (9), with no sort-support entry ([gist.h:29-37](../raw/postgres-12/src/include/access/gist.h#L29-L37)). The `buffering` option is a string parsed with `strcmp`, and the insert build leaves `fillfactor` free space on each page ([gistbuild.c:127-141](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/gist/gistbuild.c#L127-L141), [gistbuild.c:153](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/gist/gistbuild.c#L153), [gistbuild.c:489](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/gist/gistbuild.c#L489)).
- PostgreSQL 14: Differs: the sorted build exists with the same selection rule as 17, but it reserves `fillfactor` free space on each page ([gistbuild.c:15-16](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/gist/gistbuild.c#L15-L16), [gistbuild.c:242-243](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/gist/gistbuild.c#L242-L243), [gist.h:40](../raw/postgres-14/src/include/access/gist.h#L40), [gistbuild.c#gist_indexsortbuild_pagestate_add](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/gist/gistbuild.c#L481-L489)).
- PostgreSQL 18: Holds; the sorted build still ignores fillfactor ([gistbuild.c:246](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/access/gist/gistbuild.c#L246), [reloptions.c:534](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/access/common/reloptions.c#L534), [gistbuild.c:468](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/access/gist/gistbuild.c#L468), [gistbuild.c:865-866](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/access/gist/gistbuild.c#L865-L866)).
- PostgreSQL 19: Holds; the sorted build still ignores fillfactor ([gistbuild.c:246](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/access/gist/gistbuild.c#L246), [reloptions.c:566](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/access/common/reloptions.c#L566), [gistbuild.c:468](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/access/gist/gistbuild.c#L468), [gistbuild.c:865-866](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/access/gist/gistbuild.c#L865-L866)).

Related: [GiST](#gist), [Operator class](#operator-class), [Storage parameter](#storage-parameter), [Fillfactor](#fillfactor)

### Grammar

**Aliases:** `gram.y`, `scan.l`, raw parser, bison, flex. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 12, 14, 17, 18, 19.

The grammar is the bison source `gram.y`. It turns the tokens produced by the flex scanner `scan.l` into a raw [parse tree](#parse-tree) ([parser/README:1-14](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/parser/README#L1-L14), [gram.y:6-7](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/parser/gram.y#L6-L7)). `raw_parser` is the entry point that runs this lexical and grammatical analysis ([parser.c#raw_parser](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/parser/parser.c#L34-L42)). The build generates `scan.c`, `gram.c`, and `gram.h` from these files, so the checkout contains no `gram.c` ([parser/meson.build:30-41](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/parser/meson.build#L30-L41), [meson.build#bison_kw](../raw/postgres-17/meson.build#L353-L356)). The grammar must not access the database or depend on changeable state such as `SET` variables. Anything that does belongs in parse analysis, which runs later ([gram.y:25-35](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/parser/gram.y#L25-L35)).

**Version notes:**
- PostgreSQL 12: Holds, except for the build: 12 has no Meson, and the `Makefile` generates `gram.c`, `gram.h` and `scan.c`, which ship in the distribution tarball ([parser/Makefile:30-52](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/parser/Makefile#L30-L52)). `gram.y` turns `scan.l` tokens into a raw parse tree, `raw_parser()` is the entry point, and the grammar must not access the database ([parser/README:1-14](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/parser/README#L1-L14), [parser.c:36](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/parser/parser.c#L36), [gram.y:25-35](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/parser/gram.y#L25-L35)).
- PostgreSQL 14: Holds, except for the build: 14 has no Meson, and `src/backend/parser/Makefile` generates `gram.c`, `gram.h` and `scan.c` ([parser/Makefile:51-60](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/parser/Makefile#L51-L60)). `gram.y` and `scan.l` play the same roles, `raw_parser()` is the entry point, and the grammar still must not access the database ([parser/README:11-13](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/parser/README#L11-L13), [parser.c#raw_parser](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/parser/parser.c#L42-L86), [gram.y:25-35](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/parser/gram.y#L25-L35)).
- PostgreSQL 18: Holds ([parser/README:1-14](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/parser/README#L1-L14), [parser.c#raw_parser](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/parser/parser.c#L34-L42), [parser/meson.build:30-41](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/parser/meson.build#L30-L41), [gram.y:25-35](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/parser/gram.y#L25-L35)).
- PostgreSQL 19: Holds. `gram.y` and `scan.l` still produce raw parse trees through `raw_parser()`, the build still generates `scan.c`, `gram.c` and `gram.h`, and the grammar still must not access the database ([parser/README:1-16](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/parser/README#L1-L16), [gram.y:6-7](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/parser/gram.y#L6-L7), [parser.c#raw_parser](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/parser/parser.c#L33-L42), [parser/meson.build:28-42](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/parser/meson.build#L28-L42), [meson.build#bison_kw](../raw/postgres-19/meson.build#L430-L434), [gram.y:25-35](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/parser/gram.y#L25-L35)).

Related: [Parse tree](#parse-tree), [Utility command](#utility-command), [BKI](#bki)

### Grouping sets

**Aliases:** `GROUPING SETS`, `ROLLUP`, `CUBE`, `GroupingSetsPath`, `RollupData`, `AGG_MIXED`, MixedAggregate. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 17.

Grouping sets let one query group the same rows in several ways at once and return all the results together, as if several `GROUP BY` queries were combined ([queries.sgml#queries-grouping-sets](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/queries.sgml#L1230-L1236)). `ROLLUP` and `CUBE` are shorthands that expand into lists of sets. The parser expands them and refuses more than 4096 sets ([parse_agg.c:1150-1161](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/parser/parse_agg.c#L1150-L1161)), and the [planner](#planner) expands them again in `preprocess_grouping_sets()` ([planner.c#preprocess_grouping_sets](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/plan/planner.c#L2077-L2085)).

When reading source, the key idea is the rollup: a chain of sets in which each set contains the next, which one sorted pass can compute. `extract_rollup_sets()` splits the sets into the fewest such chains, to avoid extra sorts ([planner.c#extract_rollup_sets](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/plan/planner.c#L2960-L2980)). Each chain becomes a `RollupData`, which is either sorted or hashed, and a `GroupingSetsPath` carries the list ([pathnodes.h#RollupData](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/nodes/pathnodes.h#L2279-L2290), [pathnodes.h#GroupingSetsPath](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/nodes/pathnodes.h#L2292-L2304)). `consider_groupingsets_paths()` tries combinations of hashing and sorting ([planner.c#consider_groupingsets_paths](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/plan/planner.c#L4204-L4211)). A plan that uses both is strategy `AGG_MIXED`, which EXPLAIN prints as `MixedAggregate` ([nodes.h#AggStrategy](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/nodes/nodes.h#L351-L357), [explain.c:1557-1568](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/commands/explain.c#L1557-L1568)).

Related: [Planner](#planner), [Path](#path), [Upper relation](#upper-relation), [work_mem](#work_mem)

### GUC

**Aliases:** Grand Unified Configuration, configuration parameter, setting, `pg_settings`. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 12, 14, 17, 18, 19.

A GUC (Grand Unified Configuration) parameter is one server configuration setting, such as [shared_buffers](#shared_buffers) or [work_mem](#work_mem). The name comes from the "Grand Unified Configuration" scheme ([guc_tables.c:1-10](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L1-L10)). Each built-in parameter is one entry in a typed array: `ConfigureNamesBool`, `ConfigureNamesInt`, `ConfigureNamesReal`, `ConfigureNamesString` or `ConfigureNamesEnum` ([guc_tables.c:781](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L781), [guc_tables.c:2046](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L2046), [guc_tables.c:3673](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L3673), [guc_tables.c:3954](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L3954), [guc_tables.c:4754](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L4754)). An entry records the name, the [GUC context](#guc-context), the C variable, the default and the limits ([guc_tables.c#work_mem](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L2447-L2456)). A loaded library defines its own parameters at load time with `DefineCustomIntVariable()` and its siblings. They allocate the same kind of entry at run time instead of listing it in those arrays ([guc.c#init_custom_variable](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L4874-L4879), [guc.c#DefineCustomIntVariable](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L5166-L5193)). The `pg_settings` view shows each parameter's current value and context ([system_views.sql#pg_settings](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/catalog/system_views.sql#L608-L609)). It skips parameters flagged `GUC_NO_SHOW_ALL`, and it hides `GUC_SUPERUSER_ONLY` ones from users without the privileges of `pg_read_all_settings` ([guc_funcs.c#show_all_settings](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_funcs.c#L945-L950), [guc_funcs.c#ConfigOptionIsVisible](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_funcs.c#L577-L588)).

**Version notes:**
- PostgreSQL 12: Holds, except that the tables live in `guc.c`: `guc_tables.c` does not exist in 12, and the typed arrays such as `ConfigureNamesBool` and `ConfigureNamesInt` are static in `guc.c` ([guc.c:1-6](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L1-L6), [guc.c:881](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L881), [guc.c:1962](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L1962), [guc.c#work_mem](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L2231-L2240)). Custom parameters come from `DefineCustomIntVariable()` and its siblings ([guc.c#DefineCustomIntVariable](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L8579-L8606)). `pg_settings` is a view; it skips `GUC_NO_SHOW_ALL` parameters and hides superuser-only ones from users who are not members of `pg_read_all_settings` ([system_views.sql:512](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/catalog/system_views.sql#L512), [guc.c#GetConfigOptionByNum](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L9000-L9007), [guc.c#show_all_settings](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L9362-L9372)).
- PostgreSQL 14: Holds, except that the typed `ConfigureNames*` arrays live in `src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c`; 14 has no `guc_tables.c` ([guc.c:1-6](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L1-L6), [guc.c:957](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L957), [guc.c:2135](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L2135), [guc.c:2415](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L2415)). Custom parameters come from `DefineCustomIntVariable()` and its siblings ([guc.c#DefineCustomIntVariable](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L9250-L9277)). `pg_settings` is a view defined in `system_views.sql`; it skips `GUC_NO_SHOW_ALL` parameters and hides superuser-only ones from users who are not members of `pg_read_all_settings` ([system_views.sql:579](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/catalog/system_views.sql#L579), [guc.c#GetConfigOptionByNum](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L9681-L9688), [guc.c#show_all_settings](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L10043-L10053)).
- PostgreSQL 18: Holds. Built-in parameters are still entries in the typed `ConfigureNames*` arrays in `guc_tables.c`, custom ones still come from `DefineCustomIntVariable()` and its siblings, and `pg_settings` skips the same parameters ([guc_tables.c:1-10](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L1-L10), [guc_tables.c:800](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L800), [guc.c#DefineCustomIntVariable](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L5164-L5191), [system_views.sql#pg_settings](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/catalog/system_views.sql#L604-L605), [guc_funcs.c#show_all_settings](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_funcs.c#L945-L950)).
- PostgreSQL 19: Differs: the five typed `ConfigureNames*` arrays are gone. 19 has one `struct config_generic ConfigureNames[]` array, generated at build time from records in `guc_parameters.dat` by `gen_guc_tables.pl` and included into `guc_tables.c` as `guc_tables.inc.c` ([guc_tables.c:1-10](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L1-L10), [guc_tables.h:311](../raw/postgres-19/src/include/utils/guc_tables.h#L311), [gen_guc_tables.pl:1-10](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/utils/misc/gen_guc_tables.pl#L1-L10), [guc_tables.c:804](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L804)). Each record still names the parameter, its context, its variable, its default and its limits, for example `work_mem` ([guc_parameters.dat#work_mem](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_parameters.dat#L3633-L3641)). Custom parameters still come from `DefineCustomIntVariable()` and its siblings, and `pg_settings` skips the same parameters as in 17 ([guc.c#DefineCustomIntVariable](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L5073-L5098), [system_views.sql:646](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/catalog/system_views.sql#L646), [guc_funcs.c#show_all_settings](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_funcs.c#L978-L983)).

Related: [GUC context](#guc-context), [shared_buffers](#shared_buffers), [work_mem](#work_mem), [maintenance_work_mem](#maintenance_work_mem)

### GUC context

**Aliases:** `GucContext`, `PGC_POSTMASTER`, `PGC_SIGHUP`, `PGC_USERSET`. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 12, 14, 17, 18, 19.

A GUC's context says when, and by whom, a [GUC](#guc) setting can be changed. The seven values are `PGC_INTERNAL`, `PGC_POSTMASTER`, `PGC_SIGHUP`, `PGC_SU_BACKEND`, `PGC_BACKEND`, `PGC_SUSET` and `PGC_USERSET` ([guc.h#GucContext](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/utils/guc.h#L36-L76)). `pg_settings.context` shows them as `internal`, `postmaster`, `sighup`, `superuser-backend`, `backend`, `superuser` and `user` ([guc_tables.c#GucContext_Names](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L641-L650)). `set_config_with_handle()` enforces the contexts in one `switch` on the setting's context, and the `pg_settings` docs describe them ([guc.c:3474](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L3474)). An `internal` setting cannot be changed. A `postmaster` setting needs a server restart, and a `sighup` setting needs a configuration reload ([guc.c#set_config_with_handle](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L3476-L3525), [system-views.sgml#view-pg-settings](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/system-views.sgml#L3334-L3374)). A `backend` or `superuser-backend` setting is fixed for a session once the session starts. A client can set it in the connection request, for example through libpq's `PGOPTIONS`, and a change in `postgresql.conf` reaches only sessions started after the reload ([guc.c#set_config_with_handle](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L3526-L3587), [system-views.sgml#view-pg-settings](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/system-views.sgml#L3375-L3411)). A `superuser` or `user` setting can be changed with `SET` for a session or a transaction. Any user can change a `user` setting. A `superuser` setting needs a superuser or a role granted `SET` privilege on it, and a `superuser-backend` setting needs the same when the connection starts ([guc.c#set_config_with_handle](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L3588-L3611), [system-views.sgml#view-pg-settings](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/system-views.sgml#L3412-L3438), [guc.c#set_config_with_handle](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L3526-L3545)). For example, [shared_buffers](#shared_buffers) is `PGC_POSTMASTER` and [work_mem](#work_mem) is `PGC_USERSET` ([guc_tables.c:2262](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L2262), [guc_tables.c:2448](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L2448)).

**Version notes:**
- PostgreSQL 12: Holds, except that no role can be granted `SET` privilege on a parameter: only superusers can change a `superuser` setting, or set a `superuser-backend` one at connection time ([guc.c#set_config_option](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L6811-L6871), [catalogs.sgml#view-pg-settings](../raw/postgres-12/doc/src/sgml/catalogs.sgml#L10552-L10613)). The same seven contexts exist, with the same `pg_settings` names and the same restart, reload and session-start rules ([guc.h#GucContext](../raw/postgres-12/src/include/utils/guc.h#L68-L77), [guc.c#GucContext_Names](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L594-L603), [guc.c#set_config_option](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L6761-L6810), [catalogs.sgml#view-pg-settings](../raw/postgres-12/doc/src/sgml/catalogs.sgml#L10511-L10551)). In 12 the context list is documented in `catalogs.sgml`, not `system-views.sgml`. `shared_buffers` is `PGC_POSTMASTER` and `work_mem` is `PGC_USERSET` ([guc.c:2155](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L2155), [guc.c:2231](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L2231)).
- PostgreSQL 14: Holds, except that no role can be granted `SET` privilege on a parameter: only superusers can change a `superuser` setting, or set a `superuser-backend` one at connection time ([guc.c#set_config_option](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L7429-L7493), [catalogs.sgml#view-pg-settings](../raw/postgres-14/doc/src/sgml/catalogs.sgml#L12366-L12427)). The same seven `GucContext` values map to the same `pg_settings.context` names and follow the same restart, reload and session-start rules ([guc.h#GucContext](../raw/postgres-14/src/include/utils/guc.h#L68-L77), [guc.c#GucContext_Names](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L676-L685), [guc.c#set_config_option](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L7379-L7428), [catalogs.sgml#view-pg-settings](../raw/postgres-14/doc/src/sgml/catalogs.sgml#L12325-L12365)). The context list is documented in `catalogs.sgml` in 14; `system-views.sgml` does not exist. `shared_buffers` is `PGC_POSTMASTER` and `work_mem` is `PGC_USERSET` ([guc.c:2339](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L2339), [guc.c:2415](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L2415)).
- PostgreSQL 18: Holds. The same seven contexts, names and rules, including `SET` privilege for `superuser` and `superuser-backend` settings ([guc.h#GucContext](../raw/postgres-18/src/include/utils/guc.h#L40-L80), [guc_tables.c#GucContext_Names](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L657-L666), [guc.c#set_config_with_handle](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L3523-L3584), [guc.c#set_config_with_handle](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L3585-L3608), [system-views.sgml#view-pg-settings](../raw/postgres-18/doc/src/sgml/system-views.sgml#L3688-L3728), [system-views.sgml#view-pg-settings](../raw/postgres-18/doc/src/sgml/system-views.sgml#L3729-L3792)). `shared_buffers` is still `PGC_POSTMASTER` and `work_mem` still `PGC_USERSET` ([guc_tables.c:2379](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L2379), [guc_tables.c:2576](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L2576)).
- PostgreSQL 19: Holds. The seven `GucContext` values, their `pg_settings.context` names and their rules are unchanged, `shared_buffers` is still `PGC_POSTMASTER` (restart) and `work_mem` is still `PGC_USERSET` (session scope) ([guc.h#GucContext](../raw/postgres-19/src/include/utils/guc.h#L39-L80), [guc_tables.c#GucContext_Names](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L687-L696), [guc.c#set_config_with_handle](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L3435-L3496), [guc.c#set_config_with_handle](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L3497-L3520), [system-views.sgml#view-pg-settings](../raw/postgres-19/doc/src/sgml/system-views.sgml#L3900-L3940), [system-views.sgml#view-pg-settings](../raw/postgres-19/doc/src/sgml/system-views.sgml#L3941-L4004), [guc_parameters.dat:2711](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_parameters.dat#L2711), [guc_parameters.dat:3633](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_parameters.dat#L3633)). To find a 19 parameter's context, read its `context =>` field in `guc_parameters.dat`, not a C table.

Related: [GUC](#guc), [Postmaster](#postmaster)

### Hash index

**Checked on:** PostgreSQL 12, 14, 17, 18, 19.

A hash index places each entry in a bucket chosen by hashing the key. It supports only equality lookups: hash operator classes have a single strategy, equality ([stratnum.h:37-43](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/access/stratnum.h#L37-L43), [hash.c#hashhandler](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/hash/hash.c#L57-L68)). Buckets are split one at a time as the index grows, and a bucket overflows into chained "overflow pages" ([hash/README:14-29](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/hash/README#L14-L29)). Entries store only the 32-bit hash code, not the key value, and each page keeps them sorted by hash code ([hash/README:36-42](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/hash/README#L36-L42), [hash.h:466](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/access/hash.h#L466)). `hashhandler()` marks hash indexes as single-column only, with no uniqueness and no ordering, and block 0 is the [metapage](#metapage) ([hash.c#hashhandler](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/hash/hash.c#L57-L68), [hash.h:198](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/access/hash.h#L198)).

**Version notes:**
- PostgreSQL 12: Holds. Buckets split one at a time and use overflow pages, entries hold only the hash code sorted per page, `hashhandler()` sets one strategy and single-column, non-unique, unordered, and block 0 is the metapage ([hash/README:13-42](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/hash/README#L13-L42), [hash.c#hashhandler](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/hash/hash.c#L58-L68), [hash.h:196](../raw/postgres-12/src/include/access/hash.h#L196)).
- PostgreSQL 14: Holds. Buckets, overflow pages, hash-code-only entries sorted per page, one strategy, single-column and non-unique handler flags, and metapage at block 0 all match ([hash/README:14-29](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/hash/README#L14-L29), [hash/README:36-42](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/hash/README#L36-L42), [hash.c#hashhandler](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/hash/hash.c#L56-L67), [hash.h:196](../raw/postgres-14/src/include/access/hash.h#L196)).
- PostgreSQL 18: Holds. `hashhandler()` still sets one strategy, single-column, no uniqueness and no ordering, and block 0 is the metapage ([hash/README:14-29](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/access/hash/README#L14-L29), [hash.c#hashhandler](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/access/hash/hash.c#L58-L72), [hash.h:198](../raw/postgres-18/src/include/access/hash.h#L198)).
- PostgreSQL 19: Holds. Buckets still split one at a time and chain overflow pages, entries still store only the sorted 32-bit hash code, `hashhandler()` still marks it single-strategy, single-column, non-unique and unordered, and block 0 is still the metapage ([hash/README:14-29](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/access/hash/README#L14-L29), [hash/README:36-42](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/access/hash/README#L36-L42), [hash.c#hashhandler](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/access/hash/hash.c#L70-L84), [hash.h:198](../raw/postgres-19/src/include/access/hash.h#L198)).

Related: [Access method](#access-method), [Metapage](#metapage)

### Hash join

**Aliases:** `HashJoin`, `HashPath`, `Hash` node, `nodeHashjoin.c`, `nodeHash.c`, hash batches, skew optimization, Parallel Hash, `enable_hashjoin`. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 17.

A hash join reads its inner input once, builds an in-memory hash table on the join key, and then probes that table with each row of the outer input. PostgreSQL's version is a hybrid hash join ([nodeHashjoin.c:15-16](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/executor/nodeHashjoin.c#L15-L16)). It needs an equality condition whose operator is hashjoinable and that contains no volatile functions ([initsplan.c#check_hashjoinable](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/plan/initsplan.c#L3402-L3430)). The [planner](#planner) builds hash join paths in `hash_inner_and_outer()` ([joinpath.c#hash_inner_and_outer](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinpath.c#L2082-L2092)), and EXPLAIN shows a `Hash Join` over a `Hash` node ([explain.c:1444-1445](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/commands/explain.c#L1444-L1445), [explain.c:1619-1620](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/commands/explain.c#L1619-L1620)).

The table may use `work_mem` times `hash_mem_multiplier` ([nodeHash.c#get_hash_memory_limit](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/executor/nodeHash.c#L3601-L3613)). A larger inner input is split into batches that are processed one at a time. The planner estimates the batch count and charges the extra sequential I/O ([costsize.c#initial_cost_hashjoin-batches](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L4129-L4155)); the executor measures the real size and doubles the batch count when the table grows too large ([nodeHashjoin.c:26-36](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/executor/nodeHashjoin.c#L26-L36)). Inner rows whose hash value matches one of the outer side's most common values go into a small skew table, handled with the first batch, that never spills ([hashjoin.h:95-121](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/executor/hashjoin.h#L95-L121)). With Parallel Hash, workers build one shared table when both inputs have [partial paths](#partial-path) and `enable_parallel_hash` is on ([joinpath.c:2280-2292](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/joinpath.c#L2280-L2292)).

Related: [Nested loop join](#nested-loop-join), [Merge join](#merge-join), [work_mem](#work_mem), [Parallel query](#parallel-query), [Most common values and histogram](#most-common-values-and-histogram), [disable_cost](#disable_cost)

### Hash splitpoint

**Aliases:** hash split point, splitpoint group, splitpoint phase, `hashm_spares`, `hashm_ovflpoint`, `_hash_alloc_buckets`. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 17.

A splitpoint is a batch of primary bucket pages that a [hash index](#hash-index) allocates at once. Bucket pages come in power-of-2 groups called splitpoints, so each new group doubles the number of buckets. From group 10 on, a group is allocated in four equal phases, and the next phase is allocated only after the buckets of the previous one are in use ([hash/README:60-79](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/hash/README#L60-L79)). The bucket pages of one phase sit next to each other in the file. The [metapage](#metapage)'s `hashm_spares[]` array records how many overflow pages come before each phase, so a bucket's block number is computed from its bucket number ([hash/README:80-95](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/hash/README#L80-L95)). An index build estimates the size it needs and allocates enough phases at once ([hash/README:96-99](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/hash/README#L96-L99)).

Allocating a phase writes only its last page. `_hash_alloc_buckets()` extends the file's end to the end of the new phase by writing one initialized page there and expects the pages in between to read as zeroes, so on a filesystem that allows holes they may not be allocated yet ([hashpage.c#_hash_alloc_buckets](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/hash/hashpage.c#L967-L1037), [hash/README:113-123](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/hash/README#L113-L123)). A hash index's file size therefore jumps by whole phases, and part of the jump may be unused capacity rather than written pages.

A hash splitpoint is unrelated to the split point of a B-tree [page split](#page-split), which is the position at which `_bt_findsplitloc()` divides one full page between its two halves ([nbtsplitloc.c#_bt_findsplitloc](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/nbtree/nbtsplitloc.c#L86-L100)).

Related: [Hash index](#hash-index), [Relation size functions](#relation-size-functions), [Page split](#page-split)

### Heap

**Aliases:** heap table, heap access method, `heapam`. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 12, 14, 17, 18, 19.

The heap is the storage that holds a table's rows. It lives in the main [fork](#fork) of the table's files ([glossary.sgml#glossary-heap](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/glossary.sgml#L875-L886)). "Heap" is also the name of the built-in table [access method](#access-method). Its catalog row points to the handler `heap_tableam_handler`, which returns the `heapam_methods` callback table ([pg_am.dat#heap](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/catalog/pg_am.dat#L15-L17), [heapam_handler.c#heap_tableam_handler](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/heap/heapam_handler.c#L2652-L2662)). The heap keeps no row order: even after [CLUSTER](#cluster), new and updated rows are not placed in index order ([ref/cluster.sgml:45-51](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/ref/cluster.sgml#L45-L51)). An index maps key values to the [TIDs](#tid) of row versions in the heap ([indexam.sgml:38-43](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/indexam.sgml#L38-L43)).

**Version notes:**
- PostgreSQL 12: Holds. 12 is the first release with table access methods, and `heap` is the only one, with handler `heap_tableam_handler` ([release-12.sgml:5745-5756](../raw/postgres-12/doc/src/sgml/release-12.sgml#L5745-L5756), [pg_am.dat#heap](../raw/postgres-12/src/include/catalog/pg_am.dat#L15-L17), [heapam_handler.c:2666](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/heap/heapam_handler.c#L2666)). `CLUSTER` is a one-time ordering, and an index maps keys to heap TIDs ([ref/cluster.sgml:44-48](../raw/postgres-12/doc/src/sgml/ref/cluster.sgml#L44-L48), [indexam.sgml:38-42](../raw/postgres-12/doc/src/sgml/indexam.sgml#L38-L42)). 12 has no `glossary.sgml` definition.
- PostgreSQL 14: Holds. `heap` is the only table AM, its handler `heap_tableam_handler` returns `heapam_methods`, `CLUSTER` order is not maintained, and indexes store TIDs ([glossary.sgml#glossary-heap](../raw/postgres-14/doc/src/sgml/glossary.sgml#L711-L722), [pg_am.dat#heap](../raw/postgres-14/src/include/catalog/pg_am.dat#L15-L17), [heapam_handler.c#heap_tableam_handler](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/heap/heapam_handler.c#L2605-L2609), [ref/cluster.sgml:49-52](../raw/postgres-14/doc/src/sgml/ref/cluster.sgml#L49-L52), [indexam.sgml:39-40](../raw/postgres-14/doc/src/sgml/indexam.sgml#L39-L40)).
- PostgreSQL 18: Holds ([glossary.sgml#glossary-heap](../raw/postgres-18/doc/src/sgml/glossary.sgml#L900-L911), [pg_am.dat#heap](../raw/postgres-18/src/include/catalog/pg_am.dat#L15-L17), [heapam_handler.c#heap_tableam_handler](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/access/heap/heapam_handler.c#L2675-L2685)).
- PostgreSQL 19: Holds. The heap still lives in the main fork, `heap` is still the table AM whose handler returns `heapam_methods`, and indexes still map keys to heap TIDs ([glossary.sgml#glossary-heap](../raw/postgres-19/doc/src/sgml/glossary.sgml#L932-L944), [pg_am.dat#heap](../raw/postgres-19/src/include/catalog/pg_am.dat#L15-L17), [heapam_handler.c#heap_tableam_handler](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/access/heap/heapam_handler.c#L2723-L2726), [indexam.sgml:37-44](../raw/postgres-19/doc/src/sgml/indexam.sgml#L37-L44)). `CLUSTER` is now equivalent to `REPACK` with a `USING INDEX` clause, and the "no row order after clustering" note lives in the `REPACK` reference page ([ref/cluster.sgml:35-39](../raw/postgres-19/doc/src/sgml/ref/cluster.sgml#L35-L39), [ref/repack.sgml:112-119](../raw/postgres-19/doc/src/sgml/ref/repack.sgml#L112-L119)).

Related: [Access method](#access-method), [Page](#page), [TID](#tid), [Tuple](#tuple)

### Heavyweight lock

**Aliases:** regular lock, lmgr lock, table-level lock. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 12, 14, 17, 18, 19.

A heavyweight lock, also called a regular lock, is a lock taken through the lock manager (`lmgr`), which PostgreSQL uses for all user-driven locks, such as locks on tables and other database objects ([lmgr/README:32-35](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/storage/lmgr/README#L32-L35)). It has eight [lock modes](#lock-mode) with table-driven conflicts, and it detects [deadlocks](#deadlock) ([lockdefs.h:34-47](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/storage/lockdefs.h#L34-L47), [lock.c#LockConflicts](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/storage/lmgr/lock.c#L64-L104)). By default a lock is released at transaction end. Session-level locks, such as those taken by `LockRelationIdForSession()` and session-level advisory locks, last until they are released or the session ends ([lmgr.c#LockRelationIdForSession](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/storage/lmgr/lmgr.c#L374-L380), [lmgr/README:78-86](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/storage/lmgr/README#L78-L86), [lmgr/README:696-701](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/storage/lmgr/README#L696-L701)). A `LOCKTAG` names the locked object ([lock.h#LOCKTAG](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/storage/lock.h#L164-L172)). Wrappers such as `LockRelationOid()` call `LockAcquireExtended()` ([lmgr.c#LockRelationOid](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/storage/lmgr/lmgr.c#L102-L116)). Unlike an [LWLock](#lwlock), a heavyweight lock has deadlock detection and is normally held until transaction end ([lmgr/README:20-35](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/storage/lmgr/README#L20-L35)).

**Version notes:**
- PostgreSQL 12: Holds. The README describes regular locks with table-driven modes, deadlock detection and release at transaction end, plus session-level user locks; LWLocks have no deadlock detection ([lmgr/README:20-35](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/storage/lmgr/README#L20-L35), [lmgr/README:698-703](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/storage/lmgr/README#L698-L703)). `LockConflicts`, `LOCKTAG`, `LockRelationIdForSession()` and `LockRelationOid()` calling `LockAcquireExtended()` match ([lock.c:65](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/storage/lmgr/lock.c#L65), [lock.h:164](../raw/postgres-12/src/include/storage/lock.h#L164), [lmgr.c#LockRelationIdForSession](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/storage/lmgr/lmgr.c#L356-L362), [lmgr.c#LockRelationOid](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/storage/lmgr/lmgr.c#L108-L116), [lockdefs.h:34-46](../raw/postgres-12/src/include/storage/lockdefs.h#L34-L46)).
- PostgreSQL 14: Holds. Regular locks have eight table-driven modes, deadlock detection, release at transaction end by default and session-level variants; `LOCKTAG` names the object and `LockRelationOid()` calls `LockAcquireExtended()` ([lmgr/README:20-35](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/storage/lmgr/README#L20-L35), [lmgr/README:696-701](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/storage/lmgr/README#L696-L701), [lockdefs.h:34-47](../raw/postgres-14/src/include/storage/lockdefs.h#L34-L47), [lock.c#LockConflicts](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/storage/lmgr/lock.c#L65-L105), [lock.h#LOCKTAG](../raw/postgres-14/src/include/storage/lock.h#L167-L175), [lmgr.c#LockRelationIdForSession](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/storage/lmgr/lmgr.c#L351-L357), [lmgr.c#LockRelationOid](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/storage/lmgr/lmgr.c#L109-L117)).
- PostgreSQL 18: Holds. `LockRelationOid()` still calls `LockAcquireExtended()`, which gains one argument in 18, `logLockFailure` ([lmgr/README:20-35](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/storage/lmgr/README#L20-L35), [lock.c#LockConflicts](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/storage/lmgr/lock.c#L65-L105), [lmgr.c#LockRelationOid](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/storage/lmgr/lmgr.c#L101-L116), [lock.c#LockAcquireExtended](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/storage/lmgr/lock.c#L835-L841), [lmgr.c#LockRelationIdForSession](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/storage/lmgr/lmgr.c#L378-L384)).
- PostgreSQL 19: Holds. It still has eight table-driven modes, deadlock detection, release at transaction end by default and session-level locks, and `LockRelationOid()` still calls `LockAcquireExtended()`, which takes the `logLockFailure` argument as in 18 ([lmgr/README:20-35](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/storage/lmgr/README#L20-L35), [lockdefs.h:34-48](../raw/postgres-19/src/include/storage/lockdefs.h#L34-L48), [lock.c#LockConflicts](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/storage/lmgr/lock.c#L68-L108), [lmgr.c#LockRelationOid](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/storage/lmgr/lmgr.c#L107-L116), [lock.c#LockAcquireExtended](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/storage/lmgr/lock.c#L865-L871), [lmgr.c#LockRelationIdForSession](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/storage/lmgr/lmgr.c#L378-L384)). `LOCKTAG` moved from `lock.h` to a new header, `locktag.h` ([locktag.h#LOCKTAG](../raw/postgres-19/src/include/storage/locktag.h#L64-L72)).

Related: [AccessExclusiveLock](#accessexclusivelock), [ShareUpdateExclusiveLock](#shareupdateexclusivelock), [LWLock](#lwlock)

### Hint bits

**Aliases:** `HEAP_XMIN_COMMITTED`, `HEAP_XMIN_INVALID`, `HEAP_XMAX_COMMITTED`, `HEAP_XMAX_INVALID`, `SetHintBits()`, `MarkBufferDirtyHint()`. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 12, 14, 17, 18, 19.

Hint bits are flag bits in a heap [tuple](#tuple)'s header that record whether the transactions that inserted and deleted it committed or aborted, so later visibility checks can skip looking those transactions up in the commit log. `HEAP_XMIN_COMMITTED`, `HEAP_XMIN_INVALID`, `HEAP_XMAX_COMMITTED` and `HEAP_XMAX_INVALID` live in `t_infomask`, and both xmin bits together mean the tuple is frozen ([htup_details.h:204-208](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/access/htup_details.h#L204-L208)). The `HeapTupleSatisfies*` visibility routines set them as a side effect once they learn a transaction's outcome, and then call `MarkBufferDirtyHint()` on the page ([heapam_visibility.c:6-11](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/heap/heapam_visibility.c#L6-L11)). That call makes the buffer [dirty](#dirty-buffer) without logging the change; it may write a [full-page image](#full-page-image), and only when `XLogHintBitIsNeeded()`, that is when [data checksums](#data-checksums) or `wal_log_hints` are on ([bufmgr.c:5036-5049](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/storage/buffer/bufmgr.c#L5036-L5049), [bufmgr.c:5090-5100](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/storage/buffer/bufmgr.c#L5090-L5100), [xlog.h:118](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/access/xlog.h#L118)). `wal_log_hints` has context `postmaster`, so changing it needs a restart ([guc_tables.c:1170-1178](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L1170-L1178)). `SetHintBits()` refuses to set a committed hint on a permanent relation while the commit record might not be durable: it asks `TransactionIdGetCommitLSN()` for an LSN and skips the hint when `XLogNeedsFlush()` says that LSN is not flushed and the page's own LSN is older ([heapam_visibility.c#SetHintBits](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/heap/heapam_visibility.c#L82-L132)). With [asynchronous commit](#asynchronous-commit) that window is real, and it can outlast the transaction's own commit record, because the commit log stores one LSN per group of 32 transaction IDs ([clog.c:719-730](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/transam/clog.c#L719-L730)). VACUUM marks a heap page all-visible only if every live tuple on it carries `HEAP_XMIN_COMMITTED`, a check whose comment names asynchronous commit as the reason ([pruneheap.c:1371-1387](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/heap/pruneheap.c#L1371-L1387), [vacuumlazy.c:1524-1556](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c#L1524-L1556)). A page whose tuples were committed asynchronously, and whose commit LSN is not yet flushed when VACUUM reaches it, therefore stays out of the [visibility map](#visibility-map) until VACUUM examines it again after the flush, and an [index-only scan](#index-only-scan) has to visit the heap for every entry that points into it ([nodeIndexonlyscan.c:161-170](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/executor/nodeIndexonlyscan.c#L161-L170)).

**Version notes:**
- PostgreSQL 12: Holds. ### Hook

**Aliases:** `ProcessUtility_hook`, `planner_hook`, `_PG_init`. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 12, 14, 17, 18, 19.

A hook is a global function-pointer variable that core code checks at a fixed point. When a loaded library has set the pointer, core calls the library's function there. Some hooks replace a standard routine: `ProcessUtility` calls `ProcessUtility_hook` when it is set and `standard_ProcessUtility` otherwise ([utility.c:513-525](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/tcop/utility.c#L513-L525), [utility.h:71-78](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/tcop/utility.h#L71-L78)), and `planner` treats `planner_hook` the same way ([planner.c#planner](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/plan/planner.c#L274-L285)). Other hooks run in addition to core work: `post_parse_analyze_hook` runs after parse analysis, and `get_relation_info_hook` runs after the planner has read a table's catalog information ([analyze.c#parse_analyze_fixedparams](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/parser/analyze.c#L120-L127), [plancat.c#get_relation_info](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/plancat.c#L570-L576)). A library normally sets its hooks in `_PG_init()`, which runs when the library is loaded ([dfmgr.c:284-289](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/fmgr/dfmgr.c#L284-L289)). A hook function normally chains to the previous hook or to the `standard_` routine. `pg_stat_statements` saves the old `ProcessUtility_hook` in its `_PG_init()` and calls it, or `standard_ProcessUtility` when none was set ([pg_stat_statements.c#_PG_init](../raw/postgres-17/contrib/pg_stat_statements/pg_stat_statements.c#L479-L480), [pg_stat_statements.c:1157-1164](../raw/postgres-17/contrib/pg_stat_statements/pg_stat_statements.c#L1157-L1164)). A hook is a plain C variable declared in a header, with no catalog row, unlike an [event trigger](#event-trigger), which is stored in the `pg_event_trigger` catalog ([utility.h:78](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/tcop/utility.h#L78), [pg_event_trigger.h#FormData_pg_event_trigger](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/catalog/pg_event_trigger.h#L29-L43)).

### HOT

**Aliases:** heap-only tuple, HOT update, HOT chain, `HEAP_ONLY_TUPLE`, `HEAP_HOT_UPDATED`. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 12, 14, 17, 18, 19.

A HOT (heap-only tuple) update writes the new row version on the same heap page and adds no new entries to indexes that point at individual rows. The index keeps pointing at the chain's first version, and later versions are found by following the chain ([README.HOT:53-60](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/heap/README.HOT#L53-L60)). `heap_update()` chooses HOT only when the new version fits on the same page and no column of a HOT-blocking index changed. Summarizing indexes such as [BRIN](#brin) do not block HOT, but they are still updated when their columns change ([heapam.c#heap_update](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/heap/heapam.c#L4138-L4160), [README.HOT:41-46](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/heap/README.HOT#L41-L46)). The tuple header flags `HEAP_HOT_UPDATED` (on the old version) and `HEAP_ONLY_TUPLE` (on the new version) mark the chain ([htup_details.h#HEAP_ONLY_TUPLE](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/access/htup_details.h#L274-L282)). Here an "indexed column" also includes a column that appears only in a [partial-index](#partial-index) predicate ([README.HOT:36-39](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/heap/README.HOT#L36-L39)).

**Version notes:**
- PostgreSQL 12: Differs: 12 has no summarizing-index exception. `heap_update()` takes `INDEX_ATTR_BITMAP_ALL`, so a change to any indexed column, including a BRIN-indexed one, blocks HOT ([heapam.c#heap_update](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/heap/heapam.c#L2960-L2965)). The chain mechanics, the `HEAP_HOT_UPDATED`/`HEAP_ONLY_TUPLE` flags and the partial-predicate rule are the same ([README.HOT:34-38](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/heap/README.HOT#L34-L38), [htup_details.h#HEAP_ONLY_TUPLE](../raw/postgres-12/src/include/access/htup_details.h#L280-L281)).
- PostgreSQL 14: Differs: 14 has no summarizing-index exception. `heap_update()` builds its HOT-blocking set from every indexed column (`INDEX_ATTR_BITMAP_ALL`), so a change to a BRIN-indexed column also prevents HOT ([heapam.c:3287](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/heap/heapam.c#L3287), [heapam.c#heap_update](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/heap/heapam.c#L3980-L3986)). The HOT chain, the flags and the partial-predicate rule match ([README.HOT:34-38](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/heap/README.HOT#L34-L38), [htup_details.h#HEAP_ONLY_TUPLE](../raw/postgres-14/src/include/access/htup_details.h#L280-L281)).
- PostgreSQL 18: Holds ([README.HOT:53-60](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/access/heap/README.HOT#L53-L60), [README.HOT:41-46](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/access/heap/README.HOT#L41-L46), [heapam.c#heap_update](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/access/heap/heapam.c#L4114-L4136), [htup_details.h#HEAP_ONLY_TUPLE](../raw/postgres-18/src/include/access/htup_details.h#L288-L296)).
- PostgreSQL 19: Holds. `heap_update()` still chooses HOT only on the same page when no HOT-blocking indexed column changed, summarizing indexes still do not block HOT but are still updated, and `HEAP_HOT_UPDATED` and `HEAP_ONLY_TUPLE` still mark the chain ([README.HOT:34-46](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/access/heap/README.HOT#L34-L46), [heapam.c#heap_update](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/access/heap/heapam.c#L4069-L4089), [htup_details.h#HEAP_ONLY_TUPLE](../raw/postgres-19/src/include/access/htup_details.h#L295-L296)).

### Hot standby

**Aliases:** standby server, read-only replica, `hot_standby`, recovery conflict, `max_standby_streaming_delay`. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 12, 14, 17, 18, 19.

Hot standby means a server that is still replaying [WAL](#wal), as a replica or during archive recovery, also accepts read-only queries ([high-availability.sgml#hot-standby](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/high-availability.sgml#L1508-L1523)). The `hot_standby` setting turns it on. Its context is `postmaster`, so changing it needs a restart ([guc_tables.c#hot_standby](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L1797-L1800)). Replay can conflict with those queries. One example is an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock taken on the primary. Another is a vacuum cleanup record that removes rows a standby query's [snapshot](#snapshot) can still see ([high-availability.sgml#hot-standby-conflict](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/high-availability.sgml#L1759-L1791)). `ResolveRecoveryConflictWithSnapshot()` finds the conflicting snapshots ([standby.c#ResolveRecoveryConflictWithSnapshot](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/storage/ipc/standby.c#L456-L470)). Replay waits until the time the WAL was received plus `max_standby_streaming_delay`, or plus `max_standby_archive_delay` when the WAL did not arrive by streaming, and then cancels the conflicting queries. A delay of -1 means wait forever ([standby.c#GetStandbyLimitTime](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/storage/ipc/standby.c#L200-L221), [standby.c#ResolveRecoveryConflictWithVirtualXIDs](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/storage/ipc/standby.c#L380-L392)). Both delay settings have context `sighup`, so a reload applies them ([guc_tables.c:2160](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L2160), [guc_tables.c:2171](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L2171)).

**Version notes:**
- PostgreSQL 12: Holds; both settings keep the same contexts, and `GetStandbyLimitTime()` computes the same limit ([guc.c:1753](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L1753), [guc.c:2086](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L2086), [standby.c:294](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/storage/ipc/standby.c#L294), [standby.c#GetStandbyLimitTime](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/storage/ipc/standby.c#L154-L175), [high-availability.sgml:1665](../raw/postgres-12/doc/src/sgml/high-availability.sgml#L1665)).
- PostgreSQL 14: Holds ([guc.c:1905](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L1905), [guc.c:2259](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L2259), [standby.c:444](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/storage/ipc/standby.c#L444), [standby.c#GetStandbyLimitTime](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/storage/ipc/standby.c#L177-L198), [high-availability.sgml:1736](../raw/postgres-14/doc/src/sgml/high-availability.sgml#L1736)).
- PostgreSQL 18: Holds ([guc_tables.c:1896](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L1896), [guc_tables.c:2288](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L2288), [standby.c:468](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/storage/ipc/standby.c#L468), [standby.c#GetStandbyLimitTime](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/storage/ipc/standby.c#L201-L222)).

### HOT-blocking column

**Aliases:** HOT-blocking attribute, `INDEX_ATTR_BITMAP_HOT_BLOCKING`, `hot_attrs`, `hotblockingattrs`, summarized column (contrast), `INDEX_ATTR_BITMAP_SUMMARIZED`. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 17.

A HOT-blocking column is a table column that a non-summarizing index uses anywhere: as a key or included column, inside an index expression, or in a partial-index predicate. An `UPDATE` that changes one cannot be a [HOT](#hot) update. `RelationGetIndexAttrBitmap()` builds the set from every index on the table ([relcache.c#RelationGetIndexAttrBitmap](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/cache/relcache.c#L5232-L5249), [relcache.c#RelationGetIndexAttrBitmap-attrs](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/cache/relcache.c#L5400-L5442)). The columns of an index whose access method sets `amsummarizing` go into a separate summarized set instead, because such an index does not block HOT ([relcache.c#RelationGetIndexAttrBitmap-summarizing](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/cache/relcache.c#L5390-L5398)); BRIN is the in-core [summarizing index](#summarizing-index) access method ([brin.c:269](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/brin/brin.c#L269)).

`heap_update()` fetches both sets ([heapam.c#heap_update-index-attrs](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/heap/heapam.c#L3434-L3437)). When the new row version stays on the old page and no HOT-blocking column changed, the update is HOT, and only the summarizing indexes get new entries if a summarized column changed ([heapam.c#heap_update-hot-decision](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/heap/heapam.c#L4140-L4166)). Otherwise every index that accepts the new row gets an entry, including indexes whose own columns did not change ([execIndexing.c#ExecInsertIndexTuples-loop](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/executor/execIndexing.c#L343-L387)). That is why updating any HOT-blocking column adds version-churn entries to unrelated B-trees.

Related: [HOT](#hot), [Summarizing index](#summarizing-index), [Bottom-up index deletion](#bottom-up-index-deletion), [Bloat](#bloat), [Partial index](#partial-index)

### Huge pages

**Aliases:** `huge_pages`, `huge_page_size`, `MAP_HUGETLB`. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 12, 14, 17, 18, 19.

Huge pages are operating-system memory pages larger than the normal page size. Using them for the main shared memory area gives smaller page tables and less CPU time spent on memory management ([config.sgml#guc-huge-pages](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/config.sgml#L1724-L1726)). The `huge_pages` setting accepts `off`, `on` or `try` and defaults to `try`, and `huge_page_size` picks the size. Both have GUC context `postmaster`, so a change needs a restart ([guc_tables.c#huge_pages](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L5056-L5064), [guc_tables.c#huge_pages_options](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L363-L374), [guc_tables.c#huge_page_size](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L3597-L3607)). A `huge_page_size` of 0, the default, means the system's default huge page size. `GetHugePageSize()` reads that size from `/proc/meminfo` on Linux and assumes 2 MB when it cannot find it ([config.sgml#guc-huge-page-size](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/config.sgml#L1766-L1772), [sysv_shmem.c#GetHugePageSize](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/port/sysv_shmem.c#L490-L541)). In the Unix implementation, `sysv_shmem.c`, huge pages are used only when `shared_memory_type` is `mmap`, the default outside Windows and `EXEC_BACKEND` builds ([pg_shmem.h:74-80](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/storage/pg_shmem.h#L74-L80), [sysv_shmem.c:748-755](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/port/sysv_shmem.c#L748-L755)). There, on a platform that defines `MAP_HUGETLB`, `CreateAnonymousSegment()` rounds the request up to the huge page size and asks for `MAP_HUGETLB`. With `try`, it falls back to normal pages when that fails, and it records the outcome in `huge_pages_status` ([sysv_shmem.c#CreateAnonymousSegment](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/port/sysv_shmem.c#L597-L649)). That setting has context `internal`, so it is read-only ([guc_tables.c#huge_pages_status](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L5068-L5076)). With `on`, `PGSharedMemoryCreate()` raises an error instead when the platform lacks `MAP_HUGETLB` or `shared_memory_type` is not `mmap` ([sysv_shmem.c#PGSharedMemoryCreate](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/port/sysv_shmem.c#L720-L732)). Windows builds request large pages in `win32_shmem.c` instead ([win32_shmem.c:236-256](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/port/win32_shmem.c#L236-L256)).

**Version notes:**
- PostgreSQL 12: Differs: 12 has neither `huge_page_size` nor `huge_pages_status`, and `huge_pages = on` with a non-`mmap` `shared_memory_type` raises no error. `huge_pages` accepts `off`, `on` or `try`, defaults to `try`, and is `PGC_POSTMASTER` (restart) ([guc.c#huge_pages](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L4471-L4478), [guc.c#huge_pages_options](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L403-L413)). `GetHugePageSize()` always uses the system default, read from `/proc/meminfo` on Linux, or 2 MB ([sysv_shmem.c#GetHugePageSize](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/port/sysv_shmem.c#L474-L517)). `CreateAnonymousSegment()` asks for `MAP_HUGETLB` at that size and, with `try`, falls back after a DEBUG1 message ([sysv_shmem.c#CreateAnonymousSegment](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/port/sysv_shmem.c#L539-L570)). `PGSharedMemoryCreate()` rejects `on` only when `MAP_HUGETLB` is missing, and its SysV branch simply creates the segment without huge pages ([sysv_shmem.c#PGSharedMemoryCreate](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/port/sysv_shmem.c#L634-L657)). The docs give the same page-table rationale ([config.sgml#guc-huge-pages](../raw/postgres-12/doc/src/sgml/config.sgml#L1533-L1560)).
- PostgreSQL 14: Holds, except that 14 has no `huge_pages_status`: `CreateAnonymousSegment()` rounds the request up, asks for `MAP_HUGETLB` and falls back under `try` without recording a status ([sysv_shmem.c#CreateAnonymousSegment](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/port/sysv_shmem.c#L578-L610)). `huge_pages` (`off`/`on`/`try`, default `try`) and `huge_page_size` are both `PGC_POSTMASTER`, so a change needs a restart ([guc.c#huge_pages](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L4918-L4925), [guc.c#huge_page_size](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L3514-L3521), [guc.c#huge_pages_options](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/utils/misc/guc.c#L466-L477)). A `huge_page_size` of 0 means the system default, else 2 MB ([config.sgml#guc-huge-page-size](../raw/postgres-14/doc/src/sgml/config.sgml#L1726-L1732), [sysv_shmem.c#GetHugePageSize](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/port/sysv_shmem.c#L489-L540)). `on` fails at startup without `MAP_HUGETLB` or with a non-`mmap` `shared_memory_type` ([sysv_shmem.c#PGSharedMemoryCreate](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/port/sysv_shmem.c#L681-L693)). The docs give the same page-table rationale ([config.sgml:1685](../raw/postgres-14/doc/src/sgml/config.sgml#L1685)).
- PostgreSQL 18: Holds. `huge_pages` and `huge_page_size` are still `postmaster` context (restart), 0 still means the system default, and `GetHugePageSize()`, `CreateAnonymousSegment()`, the read-only `huge_pages_status` and the startup errors are unchanged ([config.sgml#guc-huge-pages](../raw/postgres-18/doc/src/sgml/config.sgml#L1801-L1803), [config.sgml#guc-huge-page-size](../raw/postgres-18/doc/src/sgml/config.sgml#L1843-L1849), [guc_tables.c#huge_pages](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L5329-L5337), [guc_tables.c#huge_page_size](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L3804-L3814), [guc_tables.c#huge_pages_status](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L5341-L5349), [sysv_shmem.c#GetHugePageSize](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/port/sysv_shmem.c#L490-L541), [sysv_shmem.c#CreateAnonymousSegment](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/port/sysv_shmem.c#L597-L649), [sysv_shmem.c#PGSharedMemoryCreate](../raw/postgres-18/src/backend/port/sysv_shmem.c#L720-L732)).
- PostgreSQL 19: Holds. `huge_pages` still takes `off`, `on` or `try` with default `try`, `huge_page_size` 0 still means the system default, both are still `PGC_POSTMASTER` (restart), and `CreateAnonymousSegment()` still falls back and sets the `PGC_INTERNAL` `huge_pages_status` ([config.sgml#guc-huge-pages](../raw/postgres-19/doc/src/sgml/config.sgml#L1844-L1863), [config.sgml:1874](../raw/postgres-19/doc/src/sgml/config.sgml#L1874), [config.sgml#guc-huge-page-size](../raw/postgres-19/doc/src/sgml/config.sgml#L1915-L1921), [guc_parameters.dat#huge_page_size](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_parameters.dat#L1246-L1262), [guc_parameters.dat#huge_pages_status](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_parameters.dat#L1264-L1270), [guc_tables.c#huge_pages_options](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/utils/misc/guc_tables.c#L365-L376), [sysv_shmem.c#GetHugePageSize](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/port/sysv_shmem.c#L491-L542), [sysv_shmem.c#CreateAnonymousSegment](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/port/sysv_shmem.c#L600-L651), [sysv_shmem.c#PGSharedMemoryCreate](../raw/postgres-19/src/backend/port/sysv_shmem.c#L722-L734)).

Related: [shared_buffers](#shared_buffers), [GUC context](#guc-context)

### Hypothetical index

**Aliases:** `IndexOptInfo.hypothetical`, what-if index. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 17.

A hypothetical index exists only in the [planner](#planner)'s list of a table's indexes; nothing is on disk. The `hypothetical` field of [IndexOptInfo](#indexoptinfo) marks it, with the comment "true if index doesn't really exist" ([pathnodes.h#IndexOptInfo-hypothetical](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/nodes/pathnodes.h#L1186-L1187)). Core code never makes one: `get_relation_info()` sets the field to false for every catalog index ([plancat.c:461](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/plancat.c#L461)), and its [hook](#hook) is where a plugin may add a hypothetical index to the list ([plancat.c#get_relation_info_hook](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/plancat.c#L570-L576)).

Planner code that would read the index file checks the flag first. The planning-time endpoint probe skips hypothetical indexes ([selfuncs.c#get_actual_variable_range-hypothetical](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/adt/selfuncs.c#L6207-L6212)). `gincostestimate()` uses zeroed metapage statistics instead of reading them, and `brincostestimate()` assumes the default pages per range ([selfuncs.c#gincostestimate-hypothetical](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/adt/selfuncs.c#L7697-L7711), [selfuncs.c#brincostestimate-hypothetical](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/adt/selfuncs.c#L8086-L8112)).

Related: [IndexOptInfo](#indexoptinfo), [Hook](#hook), [Planner](#planner), [GIN](#gin), [BRIN](#brin)

### Incremental sort

**Aliases:** `IncrementalSort`, `IncrementalSortPath`, `nPresortedCols`, presorted keys, `enable_incremental_sort`. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 17.

An incremental sort sorts rows that are already ordered by the first few sort keys. It splits the input into groups with equal leading keys and sorts each group only by the remaining keys ([nodeIncrementalSort.c:14-19](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/executor/nodeIncrementalSort.c#L14-L19)). Because it sorts one group at a time, it can start producing rows before it has read its whole input, which especially helps a query with `LIMIT` ([nodeIncrementalSort.c:51-56](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/executor/nodeIncrementalSort.c#L51-L56)).

In the [planner](#planner), an `IncrementalSortPath` is a sort path plus `nPresortedCols`, the number of leading keys the input already delivers ([pathnodes.h#IncrementalSortPath](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/nodes/pathnodes.h#L2206-L2216)). `create_ordered_paths()` uses a full sort when an input has no presorted keys and an incremental sort when it has some, unless `enable_incremental_sort` is off ([planner.c#create_ordered_paths-incremental](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/plan/planner.c#L5345-L5377)). `cost_incremental_sort()` estimates how many groups the leading keys form and prices sorting one group ([costsize.c#cost_incremental_sort](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L1973-L1984)). The executor has two modes: it sorts a minimum batch of rows on all keys, and a heuristic switches it to sorting one whole prefix group on the remaining keys when that looks beneficial ([nodeIncrementalSort.c:58-64](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/executor/nodeIncrementalSort.c#L58-L64)).

Related: [Pathkey](#pathkey), [Tuplesort](#tuplesort), [Index scan](#index-scan), [Tuple fraction](#tuple-fraction), [Planner](#planner)

### indcheckxmin

**Aliases:** `pg_index.indcheckxmin`, index usability horizon. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 17.

`indcheckxmin` is a [`pg_index`](#pg_index) flag that makes an index unusable to some transactions for a while after it is built. Its catalog comment asks "must we wait for xmin to be old?" ([pg_index.h:43](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/catalog/pg_index.h#L43)). A new index's columns may change within an existing [HOT](#hot) chain, a "broken" chain the index cannot represent, so a non-concurrent `CREATE INDEX` makes the index usable only by transactions whose snapshots are not older than it ([README.HOT#create-index](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/heap/README.HOT#L304-L311)). The flag enforces that: a transaction may use the index only once the `xmin` of the index's `pg_index` row is older than its [TransactionXmin](#transactionxmin), so any incompatible rows in HOT chains are dead to it ([README.HOT#indcheckxmin](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/heap/README.HOT#L341-L353)).

`index_build()` sets the flag only for a non-concurrent `CREATE INDEX` that met broken HOT chains ([index.c#index_build-indcheckxmin](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/catalog/index.c#L3099-L3101)). `reindex_index()` clears it, or keeps or forces it when the rebuild met such chains ([index.c#reindex_index-indcheckxmin](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/catalog/index.c#L3800-L3850)). While the flag holds, `get_relation_info()` leaves the index out of planning and marks the plan a [transient plan](#transient-plan), so a cached plan is rebuilt once the index becomes usable ([plancat.c#get_relation_info-indcheckxmin](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/util/plancat.c#L269-L281)).

Related: [pg_index](#pg_index), [TransactionXmin](#transactionxmin), [Transient plan](#transient-plan), [HOT](#hot), [Invalid index](#invalid-index), [CONCURRENTLY](#concurrently)

### Index page recycling

**Aliases:** deleted index page, delete XID, recyclable page, `gistPageRecyclable`, `GinPageIsRecyclable`, `RecordFreeIndexPage`, `GetFreeIndexPage`. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 17.

Index page recycling is how a deleted [GiST](#gist) or [GIN](#gin) index page becomes reusable. [VACUUM](#vacuum) can delete a page that has become empty, but it cannot reuse the page at once, because a scan that already read a link to it may still arrive. So the page is marked deleted and stamped with the next [transaction ID](#transaction-id) at the moment of deletion ([gistvacuum.c#gistdeletepage](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/gist/gistvacuum.c#L640-L656), [ginvacuum.c#ginDeletePage](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/gin/ginvacuum.c#L187-L192)). A later `VACUUM` treats the page as recyclable only once that XID is older than the [xmin horizon](#xmin-horizon), and only then records it in the index's [free space map](#free-space-map) ([gistutil.c#gistPageRecyclable](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/gist/gistutil.c#L885-L908), [gistvacuum.c:298-304](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/gist/gistvacuum.c#L298-L304), [ginvacuum.c#GinPageIsRecyclable](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/gin/ginvacuum.c#L805-L829), [ginvacuum.c:766-771](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/gin/ginvacuum.c#L766-L771)).

Two consequences matter when reading a page census. A page deleted by one `VACUUM` is still not free when that `VACUUM` ends, so a count of deleted pages and a count of free pages disagree after every deletion. A [snapshot](#snapshot) older than the delete XID keeps the page unrecyclable for as long as it is held. The index free space map records only whether a page is completely free, and the GiST and GIN page allocators take a recorded page before they extend the file ([indexfsm.c:14-19](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/storage/freespace/indexfsm.c#L14-L19), [indexfsm.c#RecordFreeIndexPage](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/storage/freespace/indexfsm.c#L48-L55), [gistutil.c#gistNewBuffer](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/gist/gistutil.c#L822-L850), [ginutil.c#GinNewBuffer](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/gin/ginutil.c#L299-L335)). B-tree has its own version of this, described under [B-tree page deletion](#b-tree-page-deletion).

Related: [Free space map](#free-space-map), [xmin horizon](#xmin-horizon), [Posting tree](#posting-tree)

### Index scan

**Aliases:** Index Scan node, `IndexScan`, `nodeIndexscan.c`, plain index scan. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 12, 14, 17, 18, 19.

An index scan is the plan node that walks an index and, for each matching entry, fetches the row from the table. The rows that one index range finds can sit anywhere in the heap, so the heap side of an index scan does a lot of random access. A [bitmap scan](#bitmap-scan) instead visits the heap in physical order, and an [index-only scan](#index-only-scan) can answer from the index alone ([indices.sgml#indexes-index-only-scans](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/indices.sgml#L1099-L1123)). Entries come back in key order only when the [access method](#access-method) supports ordered scans (`amcanorder`), as B-tree does; hash and GiST do not ([nbtree.c:108](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/nbtree/nbtree.c#L108), [hash.c:64](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/hash/hash.c#L64), [gist.c:66](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/gist/gist.c#L66)). In source, `IndexNext()` loops on `index_getnext_slot()`. That asks the access method for the next [TID](#tid) with `index_getnext_tid()` and then reads the heap tuple with `index_fetch_heap()` ([nodeIndexscan.c#IndexNext](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/executor/nodeIndexscan.c#L80-L130), [indexam.c#index_getnext_slot](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/index/indexam.c#L632-L698)). Because each fetch can land on a different heap page, the [planner](#planner) charges `random_page_cost` per page fetched when index order is uncorrelated with table order. It charges mostly `seq_page_cost` when they are perfectly correlated, and interpolates by the square of the correlation in between ([costsize.c#cost_index](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L644-L660), [costsize.c:787](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L787)). Both costs come from the table's tablespace when it sets its own values ([costsize.c:638-641](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/optimizer/path/costsize.c#L638-L641), [spccache.c#get_tablespace_page_costs](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/utils/cache/spccache.c#L182-L205)). Default page costs are 1.0 sequential and 4.0 random ([cost.h:24-25](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/optimizer/cost.h#L24-L25)).

### Index vacuuming

**Aliases:** `ambulkdelete`, `amvacuumcleanup`, bulk delete, vacuum cleanup, `IndexBulkDeleteResult`. **Checked on:** PostgreSQL 12, 14, 17, 18, 19.

Index vacuuming is the part of [VACUUM](#vacuum) that removes index entries pointing at dead heap tuples. Only after that can VACUUM mark the matching dead [line pointers](#line-pointer) in the heap as unused, because no index entry may point at an unused line pointer ([vacuumlazy.c:793-800](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c#L793-L800)). Each index [access method](#access-method) provides two callbacks in its `IndexAmRoutine`: `ambulkdelete` and `amvacuumcleanup` ([amapi.h:275-276](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/access/amapi.h#L275-L276)). `ambulkdelete` scans the whole index and asks a callback, for each entry's [TID](#tid), whether to delete it. VACUUM may call it more than once if its dead-TID memory fills. `amvacuumcleanup` runs once after the bulk deletions and may do further work, such as reclaiming empty index pages ([indexam.sgml#ambulkdelete](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/indexam.sgml#L390-L434)). A plain `ANALYZE` also calls `amvacuumcleanup`, with `analyze_only` set; among core access methods only GIN does work in that mode ([analyze.c:694-716](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/commands/analyze.c#L694-L716)). In PostgreSQL 17 the heap side drives both phases from `lazy_vacuum_all_indexes()` and `lazy_cleanup_all_indexes()` ([vacuumlazy.c:1990](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c#L1990), [vacuumlazy.c:2353](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c#L2353)). Without parallel workers they call `lazy_vacuum_one_index()` and `lazy_cleanup_one_index()`, which call `vac_bulkdel_one_index()` and `vac_cleanup_one_index()`. [Parallel vacuum](#parallel-vacuum) reaches the same two functions from `vacuumparallel.c` ([vacuumlazy.c:2032](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c#L2032), [vacuumlazy.c:2387](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c#L2387), [vacuumlazy.c:2449](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c#L2449), [vacuumlazy.c:2499](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c#L2499), [vacuumparallel.c:893-897](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/commands/vacuumparallel.c#L893-L897)). The access method returns an `IndexBulkDeleteResult` with counts such as tuples removed and pages deleted or free ([genam.h#IndexBulkDeleteResult](../raw/postgres-17/src/include/access/genam.h#L75-L84)). VACUUM copies only its `num_pages` and `num_index_tuples` into the index's `pg_class` row, as `relpages` and `reltuples`, and skips even that when the tuple count is only an estimate ([vacuumlazy.c#update_relstats_all_indexes](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c#L3073-L3099)). The other counts feed the `VACUUM VERBOSE` and autovacuum log report ([vacuumlazy.c:317-318](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c#L317-L318), [vacuumlazy.c:718-730](../raw/postgres-17/src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c#L718-L730)). The [INDEX_CLEANUP](#index_cleanup) option can skip this phase ([ref/vacuum.sgml#INDEX_CLEANUP](../raw/postgres-17/doc/src/sgml/ref/vacuum.sgml#L187-L221)).

**Version notes:**
- PostgreSQL 12: Differs in the call chain: 12 has no `lazy_*_all_indexes()`, `vac_*_one_index()` or parallel vacuum. `lazy_scan_heap()` loops over the indexes one at a time, calling `lazy_vacuum_index()`, which calls `index_bulk_delete()`, and later `lazy_cleanup_index()`, which calls `index_vacuum_cleanup()` ([vacuumlazy.c:1436-1440](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c#L1436-L1440), [vacuumlazy.c:1466-1471](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c#L1466-L1471), [vacuumlazy.c:1760-1762](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c#L1760-L1762), [vacuumlazy.c:1798](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c#L1798)). `lazy_cleanup_index()` itself writes `num_pages` and `num_index_tuples` into `pg_class` unless the count is an estimate ([vacuumlazy.c#lazy_cleanup_index](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c#L1803-L1815)). The two callbacks, the `ANALYZE`-only cleanup call and `INDEX_CLEANUP` exist as in 17 ([amapi.h:213-214](../raw/postgres-12/src/include/access/amapi.h#L213-L214), [analyze.c:642-657](../raw/postgres-12/src/backend/commands/analyze.c#L642-L657), [ref/vacuum.sgml#INDEX_CLEANUP](../raw/postgres-12/doc/src/sgml/ref/vacuum.sgml#L187-L204)). `IndexBulkDeleteResult` has `pages_removed` and no `pages_newly_deleted` ([genam.h#IndexBulkDeleteResult](../raw/postgres-12/src/include/access/genam.h#L72-L81)).
- PostgreSQL 14: Differs in the call chain: `lazy_vacuum_all_indexes()` and `lazy_cleanup_all_indexes()` exist, but their `lazy_vacuum_one_index()` and `lazy_cleanup_one_index()` call `index_bulk_delete()` and `index_vacuum_cleanup()` directly. 14 has no `vac_bulkdel_one_index()`, `vac_cleanup_one_index()` or `vacuumparallel.c`; parallel vacuum runs from `vacuumlazy.c` ([vacuumlazy.c:2248](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c#L2248), [vacuumlazy.c:3059](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c#L3059), [vacuumlazy.c:3006-3007](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c#L3006-L3007), [vacuumlazy.c:3115](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c#L3115), [vacuumlazy.c:2946-2952](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c#L2946-L2952)). `update_index_statistics()` writes only `num_pages` and `num_index_tuples` into `pg_class`, skipping estimated counts ([vacuumlazy.c#update_index_statistics](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/access/heap/vacuumlazy.c#L3806-L3832)). The callbacks, the `ANALYZE`-only call and the `IndexBulkDeleteResult` fields match 17 ([amapi.h:266-267](../raw/postgres-14/src/include/access/amapi.h#L266-L267), [analyze.c:735](../raw/postgres-14/src/backend/commands/analyze.c#L735), [genam.h#IndexBulkDeleteResult](../raw/postgres-14/src/include/access/genam.h#L74-L83)).
